chapters.title: Chapter 1
paragraphs: Someone must have slandered Josef K., because one morning he was arrested although he had done nothing wrong. The cook employed by Mrs Grubach, his landlady, who brought him breakfast every morning at about eight, did not come this time. That had never happened before. K. waited a little longer, watching from his pillow the old woman who lived opposite and was observing him with a curiosity quite unusual for her; then, both puzzled and hungry, he rang. There was a knock at once, and a man he had never seen in this apartment came in. He was slim but solidly built, and wore a close-fitting black outfit furnished, like a travelling suit, with various pleats, pockets, buckles, buttons and a belt, which made it look particularly practical, although it was not clear what purpose it was meant to serve. “Who are you?” K. asked, immediately sitting half upright in bed. But the man passed over the question, as though his appearance simply had to be accepted, and merely asked in return: “You rang?” “Anna is to bring me my breakfast,” said K., trying at first, in silence, to work out who the man actually was by watching him closely and thinking it over. But the man did not expose himself to this scrutiny for very long; he turned to the door and opened it a little to tell someone apparently standing just behind it: “He wants Anna to bring him his breakfast.” A small burst of laughter came from the next room; it was impossible to tell from the sound whether more than one person had joined in. Although this could not have told the stranger anything he had not already known, he now said to K., in the tone of someone delivering a report: “That is impossible.” “That would be something new,” said K., jumping out of bed and quickly pulling on his trousers. “I want to see what sort of people are in the next room, and how Mrs Grubach intends to account to me for this disturbance.” It immediately occurred to him that he need not have said this aloud and that in doing so he was, in a sense, acknowledging the stranger's right to supervise him, but just now it did not seem important. The stranger did take it that way, however, for he said: “Wouldn't you rather stay here?” “I have no wish either to stay here or to be spoken to by you until you introduce yourself.” “I meant well,” said the stranger, and now opened the door of his own accord. The next room, which K. entered more slowly than he wished, looked at first almost exactly as it had the previous evening. It was Mrs Grubach's living room; perhaps there was a little more space than usual today in this room crammed with furniture, blankets, china and photographs, but it was not immediately apparent, especially since the main change consisted in the presence of a man sitting by the open window with a book, from which he now looked up. “You should have stayed in your room! Didn't Franz tell you?” “Well, what do you want?” said K., looking from his new acquaintance to the man called Franz, who had remained in the doorway, and back again. Through the open window the old woman was visible once more; with the truly aged person's curiosity, she had moved to the window now opposite them so that she could go on seeing everything. “I want Mrs Grubach—” said K., making a movement as though wrenching himself free of the two men, although they were standing well away from him, and preparing to go on. “No,” said the man by the window, throwing his book onto a little table and getting up. “You cannot leave. You are in custody.” “So it seems,” said K. “And why?” he then asked. “We are not assigned to tell you that. Go to your room and wait. Proceedings have been set in motion, and you will learn everything at the proper time. I am going beyond my instructions in speaking to you so helpfully. But I hope no one hears it except Franz, and he himself is being friendly towards you against all regulations. If your luck holds as well as it did in the choice of your guards, you can be confident.” K. wanted to sit down, but now saw that there was nowhere to sit in the entire room except the chair by the window. “You'll come to see how true all this is,” said Franz, approaching him together with the other man. The latter in particular towered over K. and repeatedly patted him on the shoulder. Both examined K.'s nightshirt and said that he would now have to put on a much worse shirt, but that they would keep this one along with the rest of his linen and return it if his case turned out favourably. “You're better off giving these things to us than to the storeroom,” they said, “because there is often embezzlement at the storeroom, and besides, they sell everything there after a certain time, regardless of whether the proceedings concerned have ended or not. And cases like these do go on for so long, especially lately. Of course, you would eventually receive the proceeds from the storeroom, but first of all those proceeds are small to begin with, since a sale is decided by the size of the bribe, not the size of the bid, and then experience shows that such proceeds shrink as they pass from hand to hand and from year to year.” K. paid scarcely any attention to these speeches. He did not place much value on whatever right he might still have to dispose of his possessions; it mattered far more to him to understand his situation clearly; yet in these people's presence he could not even think, for the second guard's belly—guards were surely all they could be—kept bumping against him in an almost friendly way, while, when he looked up, he saw a dry, bony face, quite at odds with the heavy body, with a prominent nose bent to one side, communicating over his head with the other guard. What sort of people were these? What were they talking about? What authority did they belong to? After all, K. lived in a state governed by law, peace prevailed everywhere, all the laws remained in force; who dared to assault him in his own home? He always tended to take things as lightly as possible, to believe the worst only when the worst happened, to make no provision for the future even when everything looked threatening. But here that did not seem right to him. The whole thing could certainly be regarded as a joke, a crude joke his colleagues at the bank had arranged for some unknown reason, perhaps because today was his thirtieth birthday; that was of course possible, perhaps he merely needed to find some way of laughing in the guards' faces and they would laugh along, perhaps they were porters from the street corner, they did not look unlike them—nevertheless, this time, almost from his first sight of the guard Franz, he had been determined not to surrender the slightest advantage he might possess over these people. K. saw very little danger in anyone later saying he could not take a joke, but he did remember—although it was not otherwise his habit to learn from experience—a few incidents, insignificant in themselves, in which, unlike his friends, he had consciously behaved carelessly, without the slightest sense of the possible consequences, and had been punished by the outcome. It must not happen again, at least not this time; if this was a comedy, he would play his part.

For the moment he was free. “Excuse me,” he said, and hurried between the guards into his room. “He seems sensible,” he heard someone say behind him. Once in his room he immediately pulled open the drawers of his desk. Everything lay in perfect order, but in his agitation he could not at once find the identity papers he was looking for. Eventually he found his cycling permit and was about to take it to the guards, but then the document seemed too insignificant, and he went on searching until he found his birth certificate. As he came back into the next room, the door opposite was just opening and Mrs Grubach was about to come in. She was visible for only a moment, for scarcely had she recognised K. when she seemed to become embarrassed, begged his pardon, disappeared and closed the door with extreme care. “Do come in,” was all K. had managed to say. Now he stood with his papers in the middle of the room, still looking at the door, which did not open again, and was only startled out of this by a call from the guards, who were sitting at the little table by the open window, eating, as K. now realised, his breakfast. “Why didn't she come in?” he asked. “She isn't allowed to,” said the tall guard. “You're under arrest, remember.” “How can I be under arrest? And in this way, of all things?” “So now you're starting again,” said the guard, dipping a slice of bread and butter into the honey jar. “We don't answer questions like that.” “You will have to answer them,” said K. “Here are my identity papers. Now show me yours, and above all the warrant for my arrest.” “Good heavens!” said the guard. “Why can't you accept your position? Why do you seem determined to provoke us for no purpose, when of all your fellow human beings we are probably the closest to you just now?” “That's how it is, do believe it,” said Franz; instead of raising the coffee cup he held to his lips, he gave K. a long look, probably meaningful but incomprehensible. Without intending to, K. became involved in a silent exchange of looks with Franz, but then he slapped his papers after all and said: “Here are my identity papers.” “What do we care about them?” the tall guard now exclaimed. “You're behaving worse than a child. What do you want? Do you think you can bring your great damned case to a speedy end by discussing identity papers and arrest warrants with us, the guards? We're low-ranking employees who can scarcely make sense of an identity document, and our only involvement in your case is to stand guard over you for ten hours a day and be paid for it. That is all we are, yet we are still capable of understanding that the high authorities we serve, before ordering an arrest like this, inform themselves very precisely about the reasons for the arrest and the person being arrested. There is no mistake in that. Our authority, so far as I know it—and I know only the lowest levels—doesn't go searching for guilt among the population; rather, as the law says, it is attracted by guilt and has to send us guards out. That is the law. Where could there be a mistake?” “I don't know that law,” said K. “All the worse for you,” said the guard. “It probably exists only in your heads,” said K. He wanted somehow to slip into the guards' thoughts, turn them in his favour or establish himself there. But the guard merely said dismissively: “You'll come to feel it.” Franz intervened and said: “Look, Willem, he admits he doesn't know the law and claims at the same time to be innocent.” “You're quite right, but there's no making him understand anything,” said the other. K. said no more. Must I, he thought, let the chatter of these lowest officials—they admit themselves that that is what they are—confuse me still further? In any case, they're talking about things they don't understand at all. Only their stupidity makes their certainty possible. A few words with someone my equal will make everything incomparably clearer than the longest conversations with these men. He walked up and down a few times in the clear space in the room; opposite, he saw the old woman, who had dragged a much older man to the window and was holding her arms around him. K. had to put an end to this spectacle. “Take me to your superior,” he said. “When he wishes it; no sooner,” said the guard who had been called Willem. “And now I advise you,” he added, “to go into your room, keep quiet and wait to see what is decided about you. Our advice is: don't scatter your thoughts on useless matters; gather yourself together, because great demands will be made on you. You haven't treated us as our helpfulness deserved. You've forgotten that whatever we may be, at least for the present we're free men compared with you, and that's no small advantage. Nevertheless, if you have the money, we're willing to fetch you a little breakfast from the café across the way.”

Without replying to this offer, K. stood still for a little while. Perhaps, if he opened the door of the following room, or even the door to the entrance hall, the two would not dare to stop him at all; perhaps forcing matters to a head would be the simplest solution to the whole thing. But perhaps they would seize him after all, and once he had been thrown down he would also have lost all the superiority over them that he still, in a certain respect, maintained. He therefore preferred the certainty of a solution that the natural course of events was bound to bring, and went back to his room without another word being spoken either by him or by the guards.

He threw himself onto his bed and took from the washstand a fine apple he had set out for his breakfast the evening before. Now it was his only breakfast and, in any case, as he assured himself with the first large bite, far better than the breakfast from the dirty all-night café which he could have obtained by the grace of the guards. He felt well and confident. True, he was missing his work at the bank this morning, but given his relatively senior position there, that was easily excused. Should he give the real reason? He intended to do so. If they did not believe him, which would be understandable in this case, he could call Mrs Grubach as a witness, or the two old people opposite, who were probably now on their way to the window facing him. K. was surprised—at least, thinking along the guards' lines, he was surprised—that they had driven him into his room and left him alone here, where he had several ways of killing himself. At the same time, of course, thinking along his own lines, he asked himself what reason he could have for doing it. Perhaps because the two were sitting next door and had intercepted his breakfast. Killing himself would have been so senseless that, even if he had wanted to, the senselessness of it would have made him incapable of doing so. Had the guards' mental limitations not been so striking, one might have supposed that the same conviction had led them to see no danger in leaving him alone. Now, if they wished, they could watch him go to a little wall cupboard where he kept some good schnapps, drain one small glass to make up for his breakfast, and designate a second to give him courage—the latter only as a precaution against the unlikely possibility that it might be needed.

Then a shout from the next room startled him so badly that his teeth struck the glass. “The supervisor is calling you,” it said. Only the shouting startled him, that short, clipped, military shouting he would never have expected from the guard Franz. The order itself was very welcome. “At last,” he called back, locked the wall cupboard and hurried straight into the next room. There stood the two guards, who drove him back into his room as though it went without saying. “What are you thinking of?” they shouted. “You want to go before the supervisor in your shirt? He'll have you thrashed, and us along with you.” “Leave me alone, damn you,” cried K., who had already been pushed back as far as his wardrobe. “If people attack me in bed, they can't expect to find me in formal clothes.” “It can't be helped,” said the guards, who always became quite calm, indeed almost sad, whenever K. shouted, thereby confusing him or, in a sense, bringing him to his senses. “Ridiculous ceremonies!” he was still muttering, but he had already lifted a jacket from a chair and held it for a little while in both hands, as though submitting it to the guards' judgment. They shook their heads. “It has to be a black jacket,” they said. K. promptly threw the jacket on the floor and said—he himself did not know in what sense he meant it—“This isn't the main hearing yet, after all.” The guards smiled, but stuck to their “It has to be a black jacket.” “If it speeds things up, that's fine with me,” said K., opening the wardrobe himself, searching for a long time among his many clothes and choosing his best black suit, a lounge suit whose fitted waist had almost caused a stir among his acquaintances; then he took out a different shirt as well and began dressing carefully. Secretly he believed he had managed to speed the whole thing up because the guards had forgotten to force him to bathe. He watched them to see whether they might remember after all, but of course it never occurred to them; Willem did not forget, however, to send Franz to the supervisor with the report that K. was getting dressed.

When he was fully dressed, he had to walk just ahead of Willem through the empty adjoining room into the room beyond, whose double doors already stood wide open. As K. knew very well, this room had recently been occupied by a Miss Bürstner, a typist who generally left for work very early and came home late, and with whom K. had exchanged little more than greetings. Now the bedside table had been moved away from her bed to the middle of the room to serve as a hearing table, and the supervisor sat behind it. He had crossed his legs and rested one arm along the back of the chair.

Three young men stood in a corner of the room looking at Miss Bürstner's photographs, which were tucked into a mat hanging on the wall. A white blouse hung from the handle of the open window. At the window opposite, the two old people were leaning out again, but their company had grown: behind them, towering well above them, stood a man with his shirt open at the chest, squeezing and twisting his reddish pointed beard between his fingers. “Josef K.?” asked the supervisor, perhaps only to draw K.'s wandering eyes towards him. K. nodded. “You must be very surprised by this morning's events?” asked the supervisor, moving with both hands the few objects lying on the bedside table—the candle and matches, a book and a pincushion—as though they were things he needed for the hearing. “Certainly,” said K., seized by the pleasant feeling of at last facing a reasonable person with whom he could discuss his situation, “certainly I'm surprised, but by no means very surprised.” “Not very surprised?” asked the supervisor, now placing the candle in the centre of the little table and grouping the other things around it. “Perhaps you misunderstand me,” K. hastened to remark. “I mean—” Here K. broke off and looked around for a chair. “I may sit down, surely?” he asked. “It is not customary,” replied the supervisor. “I mean,” K. now said without further pause, “I am certainly very surprised, but when you've been in the world for thirty years and have had to make your own way, as I have, you become hardened to surprises and don't take them too seriously. Particularly not today's.” “Why particularly not today's?” “I don't mean to say I regard the whole thing as a joke; the arrangements that have been made seem too extensive for that. Everyone in the boarding house would have to be involved, and all of you as well; that would go beyond the bounds of a joke. So I'm not saying it's a joke.” “Quite right,” said the supervisor, checking how many matches there were in the matchbox. “On the other hand,” K. went on, addressing everyone now, and wishing he could even make the three by the photographs turn towards him, “on the other hand, the matter cannot be very important either. I infer that from the fact that I am accused but can find not the slightest guilt for which anyone could accuse me. But even that is secondary; the main question is: who has accused me? What authority is conducting the proceedings? Are you officials? None of you has a uniform, unless one chooses to call your outfit”—here he turned to Franz—“a uniform, but it's more like a travelling suit. I demand clarity on these questions, and I am convinced that once they have been clarified we shall be able to take the most cordial leave of one another.” The supervisor slapped the matchbox down on the table. “You are making a great mistake,” he said. “These gentlemen here and I are entirely incidental to your case; indeed, we know almost nothing about it. We could be wearing the most regulation uniforms imaginable and your case would be no worse off. Nor can I tell you at all that you are accused, or rather I don't know whether you are. You are under arrest, that is correct; I know nothing more. Perhaps the guards have been chattering about something else; in that case it was merely chatter. But even though I am not answering your questions, I can still give you some advice: think less about us and about what is going to happen to you; think more about yourself instead. And don't make such a noise about your sense of innocence. It spoils the otherwise not at all bad impression you make. In general, too, you should be more restrained in what you say. Almost everything you said just now could have been inferred from your behaviour if you had spoken only a few words; besides, it was nothing particularly favourable to you.”

K. stared at the supervisor. Was he being given schoolroom lessons here by a man who might be younger than himself? Was his openness being punished with a reprimand? And was he to learn nothing about the reason for his arrest or who had ordered it?

He became somewhat agitated, walked up and down without anyone stopping him, pushed back his cuffs, felt his chest, smoothed his hair, passed the three gentlemen and said, “It's senseless,” at which they turned towards him and looked at him with a helpful but serious air, and finally stopped once more in front of the supervisor's table. “The public prosecutor Hasterer is a good friend of mine,” he said. “May I telephone him?” “Certainly,” said the supervisor, “but I don't know what purpose that would serve, unless you have some private matter to discuss with him.” “What purpose?” cried K., more dismayed than annoyed. “Who are you, anyway? You ask for a purpose and put on the most senseless performance imaginable. Wouldn't it move a stone? These gentlemen first assault me, and now they sit or stand around here making me perform elaborate dressage routines for them. What purpose would it serve to telephone a public prosecutor when I'm supposedly under arrest? Very well, I won't telephone.” “But do,” said the supervisor, extending his hand towards the entrance hall, where the telephone was. “Please, do telephone.” “No, I no longer want to,” said K., and went to the window. The party opposite was still at its window, and only now, because K. had come to his own, did its peaceful enjoyment of the spectacle seem a little disturbed. The old people tried to get up, but the man behind them reassured them. “There are spectators like that over there too,” K. called very loudly to the supervisor, pointing out with his forefinger. “Get away from there!” he then shouted across. The three immediately retreated a few paces, the two old people even getting behind the man, who shielded them with his broad body and, judging from the movements of his mouth, was saying something inaudible at that distance. But they did not disappear entirely; they seemed to be waiting for the moment when they could approach the window again unnoticed. “Intrusive, inconsiderate people!” said K., turning back into the room. The supervisor possibly agreed, as K. thought he could tell from a sideways glance. But it was just as possible that he had not listened at all, for he had pressed one hand flat on the table and seemed to be comparing the lengths of his fingers. The two guards sat on a trunk covered with a decorative cloth, rubbing their knees. The three young men had placed their hands on their hips and were looking aimlessly around. It was as quiet as some forgotten office. “Well, gentlemen,” K. exclaimed—for a moment he felt as though he were carrying them all on his shoulders—“judging by your appearance, my business must be finished. In my view it would be best to stop considering whether or not your conduct was justified and bring the matter to an amicable close with a handshake. If you agree, then please—” And he stepped up to the supervisor's table and held out his hand. The supervisor raised his eyes, chewed his lips and looked at K.'s extended hand. K. still believed the supervisor would take it. Instead, the man stood up, picked up a hard round hat lying on Miss Bürstner's bed and carefully put it on with both hands, as one does when trying on a new hat. “How simple everything seems to you!” he said to K. as he did so. “We should bring the matter to an amicable close, you said? No, no, that really won't do. On the other hand, I certainly don't mean that you should despair. No, why should you? You are merely under arrest, nothing more. That was what I had to tell you; I have done so, and I have also seen how you received it. That is enough for today, and we can take our leave, though only for the time being. You will probably want to go to the bank now?” “To the bank?” K. asked. “I thought I was under arrest.” K. asked with a certain defiance, for although his handshake had not been accepted, he felt increasingly independent of all these people, particularly since the supervisor had stood up. He was playing with them. If they left, he intended to run after them as far as the front door and offer them his arrest. That was why he repeated: “How can I go to the bank when I'm under arrest?” “Ah,” said the supervisor, who had already reached the door, “you misunderstood me. You are under arrest, certainly, but that is not meant to prevent you from carrying out your profession. Nor are you to be prevented from following your usual way of life.” “Then being under arrest isn't very serious,” said K., moving close to the supervisor. “I never meant otherwise,” the man said. “But in that case even informing me of the arrest hardly seems to have been necessary,” said K., moving closer still. The others too had drawn nearer. They were all now gathered in a small space by the door. “It was my duty,” said the supervisor. “A stupid duty,” said K., unyielding. “Perhaps,” replied the supervisor, “but let's not waste our time on such talk. I had assumed you wanted to go to the bank. Since you pay attention to every word, let me add: I'm not forcing you to go to the bank; I had merely assumed you wanted to. And to make that easier for you, and your arrival at the bank as inconspicuous as possible, I have kept these three gentlemen, your colleagues, here at your disposal.” “What?” exclaimed K., staring at the three in astonishment. These pale, utterly unremarkable young men, whom he still remembered only as a group by the photographs, were indeed employees of his bank—not colleagues, that was saying too much and already exposed a gap in the supervisor's omniscience, but subordinate employees of the bank they certainly were. How could K. have overlooked that? How absorbed he must have been in the supervisor and the guards not to recognise these three: stiff Rabensteiner, swinging his hands; fair-haired Kullich with his deep-set eyes; and Kaminer with the unbearable smile caused by a chronic muscle strain. “Good morning!” said K. after a little while, shaking hands with the gentlemen as they bowed correctly. “I didn't recognise you at all. Well, now we'll go to work, shall we?” The gentlemen nodded eagerly, laughing, as though they had been waiting for this all along; only when K. missed his hat, which had been left in his room, did they all run one after another to fetch it, which did suggest a certain embarrassment. K. stood still and watched them through the two open doorways; last, of course, was indifferent Rabensteiner, who had merely broken into an elegant trot. Kaminer handed him the hat, and K. had to remind himself expressly, as was often necessary at the bank too, that Kaminer's smile was not deliberate, indeed that he could not smile deliberately at all. Then, in the entrance hall, Mrs Grubach, who looked not at all particularly guilty, opened the apartment door for the whole party, and K., as so often, looked down at her apron string, which cut so unnecessarily deep into her massive body. Downstairs, watch in hand, K. decided to take a car, so as not to add needlessly to the half-hour he was already late. Kaminer ran to the corner to fetch one; the other two were plainly trying to distract K. when suddenly Kullich pointed to the doorway opposite, where the tall man with the fair pointed beard had just appeared and, at first a little embarrassed at now displaying himself at his full height, stepped back against the wall and leaned on it. The old people were probably still on the stairs. K. was annoyed with Kullich for drawing attention to the man, whom he himself had already seen and had indeed been expecting. “Don't look over there,” he snapped, without noticing how conspicuous such a manner of speaking was when addressed to independent men. But no explanation was needed either, for just then the car arrived, they got in and drove off. Then K. remembered that he had not noticed the supervisor and the guards leaving at all; the supervisor had obscured the three bank employees from his view, and now the employees had obscured the supervisor in turn. That did not show much presence of mind, and K. resolved to watch himself more closely in this respect. Yet he still turned involuntarily and leaned over the car's rear deck to see whether he might catch sight of the supervisor and the guards. But immediately he turned back again and settled comfortably into the corner of the car without even attempting to look for anyone. Although it did not seem so, he could have used encouragement just then, but now the gentlemen seemed tired: Rabensteiner was looking out to the right, Kullich to the left, and only Kaminer was available with his grin, which humanity unfortunately forbade making fun of.

That spring K. generally spent his evenings by taking a short walk after work, alone or with bank employees, if it was still possible—he usually sat in the office until nine—and then going to a beer hall, where he sat at a regulars' table with mostly older gentlemen, usually until eleven. There were exceptions to this routine, however, when, for example, the bank manager, who greatly valued his capacity for work and his trustworthiness, invited him for a drive or to dinner at his villa. In addition, once a week K. visited a girl called Elsa, who worked as a waitress in a wine bar through the night until late morning and received visitors during the day only from her bed.

But that evening—the day had passed quickly in strenuous work and many flattering and friendly birthday wishes—K. wanted to go straight home. He had thought about it during every little pause in the day's work; without knowing exactly what he meant, he felt as though the morning's incidents had caused great disorder throughout Mrs Grubach's apartment and he himself was needed to restore order. Once that order had been restored, every trace of those incidents would be erased, and everything would resume its former course. In particular, there was nothing to fear from the three bank employees: they had sunk back into the bank's large staff, and no change could be seen in them. K. had repeatedly summoned them to his office, individually and together, for no purpose other than to observe them; he had always been able to dismiss them feeling satisfied.

When he arrived at the house where he lived at half past nine that evening, he met a young fellow standing in the doorway with his legs wide apart, smoking a pipe. “Who are you?” K. asked at once, bringing his face close to the fellow's; little could be seen in the half-dark of the passage. “I'm the caretaker's son, sir,” the fellow replied, taking the pipe from his mouth and stepping aside. “The caretaker's son?” K. asked, tapping his stick impatiently on the floor. “Is there something you want, sir? Shall I fetch my father?” “No, no,” said K. There was something forgiving in his voice, as though the fellow had done something wrong but he was forgiving him. “It's all right,” he then said and walked on, but before going up the stairs he turned round once more.

He could have gone straight to his room, but as he wanted to speak to Mrs Grubach, he knocked at her door at once. She sat with a stocking she was knitting at the table, on which a pile of old stockings also lay. K. apologised distractedly for coming so late, but Mrs Grubach was very friendly and would hear no apology; she was always available to him, he knew very well that he was her best and dearest lodger. K. looked around the room. It had returned completely to its former state; even the breakfast dishes that had stood on the little table by the window that morning had been cleared away. Women's hands accomplish a great deal in silence, he thought; he might have smashed the dishes on the spot, but certainly could not have carried them out. He looked at Mrs Grubach with a certain gratitude. “Why are you still working so late?” he asked. They were now both sitting at the table, and from time to time K. buried his hand in the stockings. “There's a lot of work,” she said. “During the day I belong to the lodgers; if I want to put my own things in order, I have only the evenings.” “I suppose I've given you some unusual work today as well.” “How so?” she asked, becoming a little more animated; her work rested in her lap. “I mean the men who were here this morning.” “Oh, that,” she said, returning to her calm. “That didn't give me any particular work.” K. watched silently as she took up her knitting again. She seems surprised that I'm talking about it, he thought; she seems to think I shouldn't be talking about it. All the more important that I should. It is only with an old woman that I can talk about it. “It certainly did give you work,” he then said, “but it won't happen again.” “No, it can't happen again,” she said emphatically, smiling at K. almost sadly. “Do you mean that seriously?” K. asked. “Yes,” she said more quietly, “but above all, you mustn't take it too much to heart. All sorts of things happen in the world! Since you're speaking so confidentially to me, Mr K., I can admit that I listened behind the door a little and that the two guards also told me a few things. After all, your happiness is at stake, and I really do care about that, perhaps more than I have any right to, since I'm only the landlady. Well, I heard a few things, then, but I can't say it was anything particularly bad. No. You are under arrest, certainly, but not in the way a thief is arrested. If you're arrested like a thief, that's bad, but this arrest—. It seems to me like something scholarly; forgive me if I'm saying something foolish, it seems to me like something scholarly that I don't understand, though there's no need to understand it either.”

“What you've said isn't foolish at all, Mrs Grubach. At least I partly agree with you, though I judge the whole thing more sharply than you do and simply don't consider it anything scholarly at all, but nothing whatsoever. I was taken by surprise, that was it. If I had got up as soon as I woke, without letting Anna's failure to appear throw me off, and come to you regardless of anyone who might have stepped in my way; if, just this once, I had had breakfast in the kitchen, say, and asked you to bring my clothes from my room; in short, if I had acted sensibly, nothing further would have happened, everything that was trying to develop would have been stifled. But one is so unprepared. At the bank, for instance, I'm prepared; something like this could not possibly happen to me there. I have my own attendant there, the general telephone and the office telephone stand in front of me on my desk, people are constantly coming in, clients and employees; besides, and above all, I'm constantly in the flow of work there and therefore alert. It would positively give me pleasure to be faced with something like this there. Well, it's over, and I really didn't want to talk about it any more. I only wanted to hear your judgment, the judgment of a sensible woman, and I'm very glad we agree. But now you must give me your hand; an agreement like this must be confirmed by a handshake.”

Will she give me her hand? The supervisor didn't give me his, he thought, studying the woman with a different look from before. She stood up because he too had stood up; she was a little embarrassed because she had not understood everything K. had said. But this embarrassment made her say something she did not mean to say, something entirely out of place: “Please don't take it so much to heart, Mr K.,” she said, with tears in her voice, and of course forgot the handshake too. “I'm not aware that I'm taking it to heart,” said K., suddenly tired and seeing how worthless all this woman's agreement was.

At the door he asked one more question: “Is Miss Bürstner home?” “No,” said Mrs Grubach, accompanying this plain information with a smile of belated, sensible sympathy. “She's at the theatre. Did you want something from her? Shall I give her a message?” “Oh, I only wanted a few words with her.” “I'm afraid I don't know when she'll come back. When she goes to the theatre, she usually comes back late.” “That doesn't matter at all,” said K., already turning his lowered head towards the door to leave. “I only wanted to apologise for having made use of her room today.” “There's no need, Mr K. You're too considerate. The young lady knows nothing about it; she hasn't been home since early this morning, and everything has been put back in order. See for yourself.” And she opened the door to Miss Bürstner's room. “Thank you, I believe you,” said K., but nevertheless went over to the open doorway. Moonlight shone quietly into the dark room. As far as one could see, everything really was in its place; even the blouse no longer hung from the window handle. The pillows on the bed seemed strikingly high; they lay partly in the moonlight. “The young lady often comes home late,” said K., looking at Mrs Grubach as though she were responsible. “That's how young people are!” said Mrs Grubach apologetically. “Certainly, certainly,” said K., “but it can go too far.” “It can,” said Mrs Grubach. “How right you are, Mr K. Perhaps even in this case. I certainly don't want to slander Miss Bürstner. She's a good, sweet girl, friendly, tidy, punctual, hardworking; I value all that very highly. But one thing is true: she should have more pride, more reserve. Twice this month already I've seen her in out-of-the-way streets, each time with a different gentleman. It's very embarrassing to me; before God, I'm telling only you, Mr K., but I won't be able to avoid speaking to the young lady herself about it. Besides, it's not the only thing that makes me suspicious of her.” “You're quite on the wrong track,” said K., furious and scarcely able to conceal it. “Besides, you evidently misunderstood my remark about the young lady. That wasn't what I meant. I must even warn you earnestly against saying anything to her. You're entirely mistaken. I know the young lady very well; none of what you said is true. Then again, perhaps I'm going too far. I won't stop you. Tell her whatever you like. Good night.” “Mr K.,” said Mrs Grubach pleadingly, hurrying after him to his door, which he had already opened, “I'm not going to speak to the young lady yet. Naturally I want to observe her further first. You're the only one I've confided in about what I know. After all, it must be in every lodger's interests for someone to try to keep the boarding house clean, and that is all I'm trying to do.” “Clean!” K. called through the gap in the door. “If you want to keep the boarding house clean, you'll have to give me notice first.” Then he slammed the door and paid no further attention to a gentle knocking.

Instead, since he had no desire to sleep, he decided to stay awake and take the opportunity to find out when Miss Bürstner would come home. Perhaps then, however inappropriate it might be, he could still have a few words with her. Leaning at the window and pressing his tired eyes, he even thought for a moment of punishing Mrs Grubach and persuading Miss Bürstner to give notice together with him. But immediately that seemed terribly excessive, and he even suspected himself of trying to change lodgings because of the morning's incidents. Nothing could have been more absurd, and above all more pointless and contemptible.

When he grew tired of looking out at the empty street, he lay down on the sofa, having opened the door to the entrance hall a little so that he could see anyone entering the apartment directly from the sofa. Until about eleven he lay quietly there smoking a cigar. From then on, however, he could bear it no longer and went out into the entrance hall for a while, as though that could hasten Miss Bürstner's arrival. He had no particular longing for her; he could not even remember exactly what she looked like. But now he wanted to talk to her, and it irritated him that by coming home late she was bringing unrest and disorder even into the close of this day. It was her fault, too, that he had not eaten dinner and had missed the visit to Elsa he had intended to make that evening. He could, of course, still make up for both by going now to the wine bar where Elsa worked. He intended to do that later too, after speaking with Miss Bürstner.

It was past half past eleven when someone could be heard on the stairs. K., who had been pacing noisily up and down the entrance hall, absorbed in his thoughts as though it were his own room, fled behind his door. It was Miss Bürstner who had arrived. Shivering, she drew a silk scarf close around her narrow shoulders while locking the door. In another moment she would go into her room, which K. certainly had no right to invade at midnight; he therefore had to speak to her now, but unfortunately he had neglected to switch on the electric light in his own room, so that stepping out of the darkness would look like an attack and must at the very least give her a bad fright. Helpless, and with no time to lose, he whispered through the gap in the door: “Miss Bürstner.” It sounded like a plea rather than a call. “Is someone here?” asked Miss Bürstner, looking around with wide eyes. “It's me,” said K., stepping forward. “Oh, Mr K.!” said Miss Bürstner, smiling. “Good evening,” and she held out her hand. “I wanted to have a few words with you. Would you allow me to do that now?” “Now?” asked Miss Bürstner. “Does it have to be now? It's a little odd, isn't it?” “I've been waiting for you since nine.” “Well, I was at the theatre. I didn't know anything about you.” “The occasion for what I want to say only arose today.” “Oh. Well, I have no objection in principle, except that I'm tired enough to drop. Come into my room for a few minutes, then. We certainly can't talk here; we'll wake everyone, and I'd find that even more unpleasant for our sake than for theirs. Wait here until I've turned on the light in my room, then turn this light off.” K. did so, but then waited until Miss Bürstner quietly invited him in again from her room. “Sit down,” she said, pointing to the divan; she herself remained standing upright by the bedpost despite the tiredness she had spoken of, and did not even take off her small hat, which was laden with an excess of flowers. “So what did you want? I'm really curious.” She crossed her legs lightly. “Perhaps you'll say,” K. began, “that the matter wasn't urgent enough to discuss now, but—” “I never listen to introductions,” said Miss Bürstner. “That makes my task easier,” said K. “Your room was put into some disorder this morning, in a sense through my fault. It was done by strangers against my wishes, and yet, as I say, through my fault; I wanted to apologise for that.” “My room?” asked Miss Bürstner, examining K. instead of the room. “That's right,” said K., and now for the first time the two looked each other in the eyes. “How it happened is in itself not worth a word.” “But surely that's the interesting part,” said Miss Bürstner. “No,” said K. “Well,” said Miss Bürstner, “I don't want to intrude into secrets. If you insist it's uninteresting, I won't argue. I'm happy to grant the forgiveness you're asking for, particularly since I can't find any trace of disorder.” With her hands flat against her hips, low down, she made a circuit of the room. She stopped at the mat holding the photographs. “Look,” she exclaimed, “my photographs really have been jumbled up. That's unpleasant. So someone has been in my room without permission.” K. nodded and silently cursed the bank employee Kaminer, who could never restrain his dreary, pointless liveliness. “It's strange,” said Miss Bürstner, “that I'm forced to forbid you something you ought to forbid yourself: entering my room when I'm not here.” “But I explained to you, Miss Bürstner,” said K., going over to the photographs as well, “that I wasn't the one who tampered with your photographs. But since you don't believe me, I have to admit that the investigating commission brought three bank employees with it, one of whom—whom I'll get thrown out of the bank at the next opportunity—probably picked up the photographs.” “Yes, there was an investigating commission here,” K. added, as the young woman looked at him questioningly. “On your account?” she asked. “Yes,” K. replied. “No!” she exclaimed, laughing. “Yes,” said K. “Do you think I'm innocent?” “Well, innocent,” she said, “I don't want to pass a judgment at once that might have consequences, and I don't know you, after all. Still, it must take a serious criminal to have an investigating commission sent after him straight away. But since you're free—I assume from your calm manner, at least, that you haven't escaped from prison—you can't have committed a crime like that.” “Yes,” said K., “but the investigating commission may have realised that I'm innocent, or at least not as guilty as they supposed.” “Certainly, that could be,” said Miss Bürstner, listening very attentively. “You see,” said K., “you don't have much experience of court matters.” “No, I don't,” said Miss Bürstner, “and I've often regretted it, because I'd like to know everything, and court matters in particular interest me enormously. The court has a peculiar attraction, doesn't it? But I'll certainly fill in the gaps in my knowledge in that direction, because next month I'm starting as a clerk in a lawyer's office.” “That's very good,” said K. “Then you'll be able to help me a little with my case.” “Possibly,” said Miss Bürstner. “Why not? I like putting my knowledge to use.” “I mean it seriously, too,” said K., “or at least as half-seriously as you do. The matter is far too petty to bring in a lawyer, but I could certainly use an adviser.” “Yes, but if I'm to be your adviser, I'd have to know what it's about,” said Miss Bürstner. “That's precisely the difficulty,” said K. “I don't know myself.” “Then you've been making fun of me,” said Miss Bürstner, excessively disappointed. “There was absolutely no need to choose this late hour of the night for that.” And she moved away from the photographs, where they had stood together for so long. “But Miss Bürstner,” said K., “I'm not joking. Why won't you believe me? I've already told you what I know. Even more than I know, because it wasn't an investigating commission at all; I call it that because I don't know any other name for it. Nothing was investigated. I was only arrested, but by a commission.” Miss Bürstner sat on the divan and laughed again. “What was it like, then?” she asked. “Terrible,” said K., but he was not thinking about that now at all; he was entirely absorbed in the sight of Miss Bürstner resting her face on one hand—her elbow on the divan cushion—while her other hand slowly stroked her hip. “That's too general,” said Miss Bürstner. “What's too general?” K. asked. Then he remembered and asked: “Shall I show you how it happened?” He wanted to move about, yet not to leave. “I'm already tired,” said Miss Bürstner. “You came so late,” said K. “Now it ends with me being reproached. And rightly, too, because I shouldn't have let you in at all. As it turns out, there wasn't any need.” “There was a need; you'll only see that now,” said K. “May I move the bedside table over here?” “What are you thinking of?” said Miss Bürstner. “Of course you may not!” “Then I can't show you,” said K. in agitation, as though he were being done immeasurable harm. “Well, if you need it for the demonstration, go ahead and move the little table,” said Miss Bürstner, adding after a little while in a weaker voice: “I'm so tired that I'm allowing more than is good.” K. placed the table in the middle of the room and sat down behind it. “You have to picture the arrangement of the people correctly; it's very interesting. I'm the supervisor; over there on the trunk sit two guards; by the photographs stand three young men. From the window handle hangs a white blouse, which I mention only in passing. And now it begins. Oh, I'm forgetting myself, the most important person: I, then, am standing here in front of the little table. The supervisor is sitting extremely comfortably, his legs crossed, his arm hanging down here over the back of the chair, a lout beyond compare. And now it really does begin. The supervisor calls out as though he has to wake me; he positively shouts. Unfortunately, if I'm to make it clear to you, I have to shout too. It's only my name he's shouting, by the way.” Miss Bürstner, who was listening with laughter, put her forefinger to her lips to stop K. from shouting, but it was too late. K. was too deeply in the role. He called slowly, “Josef K.”—not as loudly as he had threatened, but still in such a way that the call, once suddenly uttered, seemed to spread through the room only gradually.

Then there were several knocks on the door of the next room, loud, short and regular. Miss Bürstner turned pale and put her hand to her heart. K. was particularly startled because for a little while he was still quite incapable of thinking of anything except the morning's events and the girl to whom he was demonstrating them. As soon as he had collected himself, he sprang over to Miss Bürstner and took her hand. “Don't be afraid,” he whispered. “I'll put everything right. But who can it be? There's only the living room next door, and no one sleeps there.” “Someone does,” Miss Bürstner whispered into K.'s ear. “Since yesterday, a nephew of Mrs Grubach's has been sleeping there, a captain. There isn't another room free at the moment. I'd forgotten it too. Why did you have to shout like that? I'm so unhappy about it.” “There's no reason to be,” said K., and as she now sank back against the cushion, he kissed her forehead. “Go away, go away,” she said, quickly sitting up again. “Please go, please go. What do you want? He's listening at the door, he can hear everything. How you torment me!” “I won't leave,” said K., “until you're a little calmer. Come to the other corner of the room; he can't hear us there.” She let herself be led there. “You're forgetting,” he said, “that although this is unpleasant for you, it presents no danger at all. You know how Mrs Grubach, who is the one who decides in this matter, particularly as the captain is her nephew, positively worships me and believes unconditionally everything I say. Besides, she is dependent on me, since she has borrowed a fairly large sum from me. I'll accept any explanation you suggest for our being together, provided it serves the purpose at all, and I guarantee to make Mrs Grubach believe it, not merely in public but genuinely and sincerely. You needn't spare me in any way. If you want it said that I attacked you, Mrs Grubach will be told that and will believe it without losing her trust in me; that's how attached she is to me.” Miss Bürstner looked silently at the floor in front of her, a little slumped. “Why shouldn't Mrs Grubach believe I attacked you?” K. added. Before him he saw her hair, parted, arranged in low puffs, held firmly together, reddish hair. He thought she would turn her eyes towards him, but without changing her position she said: “Forgive me. I was frightened by the sudden knocking, not so much by the consequences the captain's presence might have. It was so quiet after your shout, and then came the knocking; that's why I was so frightened. I was also sitting near the door; the knocking was almost beside me. Thank you for your suggestions, but I don't accept them. I can take responsibility for everything that happens in my room, to anyone at all. I'm surprised you don't notice how insulting your suggestions are to me, alongside the good intentions, of course, which I certainly acknowledge. But now go, leave me alone; I need that even more now than before. The few minutes you asked for have become half an hour and more.” K. took her by the hand and then by the wrist. “But you're not angry with me?” he said. She brushed his hand away and answered: “No, no, I'm never angry with anyone.” He reached for her wrist again; this time she allowed it and led him to the door that way. He was firmly resolved to leave. But at the door, as though he had not expected to find a door there, he stopped. Miss Bürstner used that moment to free herself, open the door, slip into the entrance hall and say quietly to K. from there: “Now please come. Look”—she pointed to the captain's door, beneath which a light was shining—“he's turned on the light and is talking about us.” “I'm coming,” said K., running forward, seizing her, kissing her on the mouth and then all over her face, like a thirsty animal racing its tongue over the spring water it has at last found. Finally he kissed her on the neck, where the throat is, and left his lips resting there for a long time. A noise from the captain's room made him look up. “Now I'll go,” he said. He wanted to call Miss Bürstner by her first name, but did not know it. She nodded tiredly and, already half turned away, left him her hand to kiss as though unaware of it, then went into her room with her back bent. Shortly afterwards K. lay in his bed. He fell asleep very soon. Before falling asleep, he thought for a little while about his behaviour; he was satisfied with it, but wondered why he was not still more satisfied. On account of the captain, he was seriously worried about Miss Bürstner.

chapters.title: Chapter 2
paragraphs: K. had been informed by telephone that a brief examination of his case would take place the following Sunday. He was told that these examinations would now follow regularly, if perhaps not every week, then at frequent intervals. On the one hand, it was in the general interest to bring the case to a swift conclusion; on the other, the examinations had to be thorough in every respect, yet, because of the strain involved, must never last too long. That was why they had chosen the solution of brief examinations following one another in quick succession. Sunday had been designated as the day for examination so as not to interfere with K.'s professional work. They assumed he agreed; if he preferred another appointment, they would accommodate him as far as possible. The examinations could, for instance, also take place at night, though K. would probably not be fresh enough then. In any event, they would keep to Sunday unless K. objected. It went without saying that he absolutely must attend; surely there was no need to point that out to him. He was given the number of the house where he was to appear. It was in a remote suburban street where K. had never been.

Having received this message, K. hung up without replying. He had immediately resolved to go on Sunday; it was certainly necessary. The case was getting under way and he had to oppose it; this first examination should also be the last. He was still standing thoughtfully by the telephone when he heard behind him the voice of the deputy manager, who wanted to make a call but found K. in his way. “Bad news?” the deputy manager asked casually, not to find anything out, but to get K. away from the telephone. “No, no,” said K., stepping aside but not leaving. The deputy manager picked up the receiver and, while waiting for his connection, said over it: “May I ask you something, Mr K.? Would you do me the pleasure of joining a trip on my sailing boat on Sunday morning? There will be quite a party, including people you know, certainly. The public prosecutor Hesterer, among others. Will you come? Do come!” K. tried to pay attention to what the deputy manager was saying. It was not unimportant to him, for this invitation from the deputy manager, with whom he had never got on particularly well, represented an attempt at reconciliation on the man's part and showed how important K. had become at the bank, and how valuable his friendship, or at least his impartiality, seemed to its second-highest official. This invitation was a humiliation for the deputy manager, even if it had merely been spoken over the receiver while he waited to be connected. But K. had to follow it with a second humiliation. He said: “Thank you very much! Unfortunately, I have no time on Sunday. I already have an engagement.” “A pity,” said the deputy manager, turning to the telephone conversation, which had just been connected. It was not a short conversation, but in his distraction K. remained beside the telephone throughout. Only when the deputy manager rang off did he start and say, in a small attempt to excuse his pointless lingering: “Someone has just telephoned asking me to go somewhere, but they forgot to tell me at what time.” “Then ask them again,” said the deputy manager. “It isn't very important,” said K., although this further weakened his earlier excuse, already inadequate in itself. As he left, the deputy manager went on speaking about other things. K. forced himself to answer too, but was mainly thinking that it would be best to arrive at nine on Sunday morning, since that was when all the courts began work on weekdays.

Sunday was overcast. K. was very tired, having stayed at the inn until late into the night for a celebration among the regulars; he had almost overslept. In a hurry, with no time to consider and put together the various plans he had devised during the week, he dressed and ran, without breakfast, to the suburb he had been directed to. Strangely, although he had little time to look around, he encountered the three bank employees involved in his affair, Rabensteiner, Kullich and Kaminer. The first two crossed his path in a tram, while Kaminer was sitting on a café terrace and, just as K. passed, leaned curiously over the railing. They were probably all watching him and wondering at the way their superior was running. Some sort of defiance had kept K. from taking transport; in this affair of his he recoiled from any outside help, however slight, and he did not want to call on anyone and thereby let them into the matter even in the remotest way; finally, he had not the slightest desire to humble himself before the investigating commission by being excessively punctual. Admittedly, he was now running simply to arrive as close to nine as possible, although he had not even been summoned for a particular hour.

He had thought he would recognise the building from far away by some sign he had not clearly pictured to himself, or by unusual activity in front of the entrance. But Juliusstraße, where it was supposed to be, and at the beginning of which K. stopped for a moment, had almost entirely uniform houses on both sides: tall, grey tenements inhabited by poor people. Now, on Sunday morning, most of the windows were occupied; men in shirtsleeves leaned there smoking, or held small children carefully and tenderly at the window ledge. Other windows were piled high with bedding, above which a woman's tousled head briefly appeared. People called to one another across the street; one such call caused loud laughter just above K. At regular intervals along the long street were little shops selling various foods, below street level and reached by a few steps. Women went in and out or stood on the steps chatting. A fruit seller calling his wares up to the windows, as inattentive as K. himself, almost knocked him down with his cart. Just then a gramophone discarded from the better districts of the city began playing with murderous loudness.

K. went farther into the street, slowly, as though he now had time, or as though the examining magistrate could see him from some window and therefore knew he had arrived. It was shortly after nine. The house was quite a way along; it was almost unusually extensive, and the entrance for vehicles in particular was high and wide. It was evidently intended for the goods wagons serving the various warehouses, now locked, which surrounded the large courtyard and bore the names of firms, some of which K. knew through the bank's business. Taking a closer interest in all these external details than was his habit, he also stopped for a little while at the entrance to the courtyard. Nearby, a barefoot man sat on a crate reading a newspaper. Two boys were rocking on a handcart. A frail young girl in a night jacket stood at a pump, looking at K. as the water flowed into her jug. In one corner of the courtyard a line was being stretched between two windows, with the washing to be dried already hanging on it. A man stood below, directing the work with a few shouted instructions.

K. turned towards the stairs to reach the examination room, but stopped again, for besides this staircase he could see three other stair entrances in the courtyard, and a small passage at the far end seemed to lead to a second courtyard as well. He was annoyed that they had not told him more precisely where the room was. It was a strange negligence or indifference with which they treated him, and he intended to state that very loudly and clearly. In the end he went up the first staircase after all, playing in his mind with the remembered remark of the guard Willem that the court was attracted by guilt, from which it really followed that the examination room must be on whichever staircase K. happened to choose.

As he climbed he disturbed many children playing on the stairs, who looked angrily at him when he walked through their ranks. “If I have to come here again,” he told himself, “I must bring either sweets to win them over or my stick to thrash them.” Just below the first floor he even had to wait a little while for a ball to finish rolling; meanwhile two small boys with the crafty faces of grown-up ruffians held him by his trouser legs. If he had wanted to shake them off, he would have had to hurt them, and he dreaded their screaming.

The real search began on the first floor. Since he could hardly ask for the investigating commission, he invented a carpenter called Lanz—the name occurred to him because that was the name of the captain, Mrs Grubach's nephew—and planned to ask in every apartment whether a carpenter called Lanz lived there, giving himself a chance to look into the rooms. But it turned out that this was usually possible without further effort, since almost all the doors were open and children ran in and out. Most were small rooms with one window, where the cooking was done as well. Some women held infants in their arms while working at the stove with their free hand. Adolescent girls, apparently wearing nothing but aprons, were the busiest, running back and forth. In every room the beds were still in use, occupied by sick people, people still asleep, or people stretched out fully dressed. At apartments whose doors were closed, K. knocked and asked whether a carpenter called Lanz lived there. Usually a woman opened, listened to the question, and turned into the room to someone getting out of bed. “The gentleman is asking whether a carpenter called Lanz lives here.” “Carpenter Lanz?” asked the person in the bed. “Yes,” said K., although the investigating commission was undoubtedly not here and his task was therefore finished. Many thought it mattered greatly to K. to find the carpenter Lanz. They reflected for a long time, named a carpenter who was not called Lanz, or a name bearing some distant resemblance to Lanz, or asked the neighbours, or accompanied K. to a door far away where they thought such a man might be subletting a room, or where someone might be able to give better information than they could. Eventually K. scarcely had to ask for himself any more, but was drawn through the floors in this way. He regretted his plan, which had seemed so practical at first. Below the fifth floor he decided to abandon the search, took leave of a friendly young worker who wanted to lead him farther up, and went down. But then the futility of the whole undertaking annoyed him again. He went back once more and knocked at the first door on the fifth floor. The first thing he saw in the little room was a large wall clock already showing ten. “Does a carpenter called Lanz live here?” he asked. “Please,” said a young woman with bright black eyes, who was washing children's linen in a bucket, pointing with her wet hand to the open door of the adjoining room.

K. thought he was entering a meeting. A crowd of all sorts of people—no one took any notice of his arrival—filled a medium-sized room with two windows, encircled just below the ceiling by a gallery that was also completely full, where people could stand only bent over, knocking their heads and backs against the ceiling. Finding the air too stuffy, K. stepped outside again and said to the young woman, who had probably misunderstood him: “I asked for a carpenter, a man called Lanz?” “Yes,” said the woman. “Please go in.” K. might not have obeyed if she had not come towards him, taken hold of the door handle and said: “I have to close it after you. No one else is allowed in.” “Very sensible,” said K., “but it's already too full.” Then he went in again nevertheless.

A hand reached for K. from between two men talking just inside the door—one was making the motion of counting out money with both hands extended far in front of him, while the other stared sharply into his eyes. It belonged to a small, rosy-cheeked boy. “Come, come,” he said. K. let the boy lead him. It turned out that a narrow passage remained clear through the milling crowd, perhaps dividing two parties; this was also suggested by the fact that in the front rows to right and left K. saw scarcely a face turned towards him, but only the backs of people directing their words and gestures solely to others of their own party. Most were dressed in black, in old Sunday coats hanging long and loose. Only these clothes puzzled K.; otherwise he would have taken the whole thing for a local political meeting.

At the other end of the hall, to which K. was led, a small table had been set crosswise on a very low platform that was also overcrowded. Behind it, near the edge of the platform, sat a short, fat, wheezing man, talking with great laughter to someone standing behind him, his elbow propped on the back of the chair and his legs crossed. Now and then the seated man threw an arm into the air as though caricaturing someone. The boy leading K. had difficulty delivering his message. Twice he had already tried, standing on tiptoe, without being noticed by the man above. Only when someone on the platform drew attention to the boy did the man turn towards him and bend down to hear his quiet report. Then he took out his watch and glanced quickly at K. “You should have appeared an hour and five minutes ago,” he said. K. wanted to reply, but had no time, for scarcely had the man finished speaking when a general murmur arose from the right half of the hall. “You should have appeared an hour and five minutes ago,” the man now repeated in a raised voice, glancing quickly down into the hall as well. The murmuring immediately grew louder, and, as the man said nothing more, died away only gradually. The hall was now much quieter than when K. had entered. Only the people in the gallery went on making their remarks. As far as anything could be distinguished up there in the dim light, haze and dust, they seemed worse dressed than those below. Some had brought cushions to put between their heads and the ceiling so as not to rub themselves sore.

K. had decided to observe more than he spoke, and therefore gave up defending himself against the allegation that he had arrived late, saying only: “I may have come late, but I'm here now.” Applause followed, again from the right half of the hall. “Easy people to win over,” K. thought, disturbed only by the silence in the left half, which was directly behind him and from which only a few isolated claps had come. He considered what he could say to win everyone over at once or, if that was impossible, at least win the others over from time to time as well.

“Yes,” said the man, “but I am no longer obliged to question you now”—again the murmuring, but this time its meaning was unclear, for the man went on, waving the people quiet—“nevertheless, as an exception, I will still do so today. But lateness like this must not be repeated. Now step forward!” Someone jumped down from the platform, freeing a space that K. stepped up into. He stood pressed close against the table; the crowd behind him was so dense that he had to resist it if he was not to push the examining magistrate's table, and perhaps the magistrate himself, off the platform.

The examining magistrate paid no attention to this, however, but sat comfortably enough in his chair and, after a final word to the man behind him, reached for a little notebook, the only object on his table. It was like an exercise book, old and completely misshapen from frequent turning of its pages. “Well, then,” said the examining magistrate, leafing through it and addressing K. in the tone of someone stating a fact, “you are a house painter?” “No,” said K., “I'm the chief authorised signatory of a large bank.” This answer was followed by laughter from the party on the right, so hearty that K. had to laugh along. People propped their hands on their knees and shook as though in severe fits of coughing. Even some in the gallery laughed. The examining magistrate, who had become thoroughly angry and was probably powerless against those below, tried to make up for it with the gallery: he sprang up and threatened it, and his otherwise inconspicuous eyebrows crowded over his eyes, bushy, black and large.

But the left half of the hall was still quiet. The people stood there in rows, their faces turned towards the platform, listening to the words exchanged above as calmly as to the noise of the other party; they even tolerated individuals from their own ranks occasionally joining in with the other side. The people of the left-hand party, who were fewer in number, might at bottom be just as insignificant as those on the right, but the calmness of their behaviour made them seem more important. When K. now began speaking, he was convinced that he was speaking in their spirit.

“Your question, Mr Examining Magistrate, as to whether I am a house painter—or rather, you didn't ask at all, but stated it to my face—is characteristic of the entire manner of the proceedings being conducted against me. You may object that these are not proceedings at all, and you are quite right, for they are proceedings only if I recognise them as such. But for this moment, then, I do recognise them, out of pity, in a sense. One can take no attitude towards them except pity, if one is to pay them any attention at all. I am not saying these are disreputable proceedings, but I would like to offer you that description for your own self-examination.”

K. broke off and looked down into the hall. What he had said was sharp, sharper than he had intended, but nevertheless correct. It deserved applause here or there, yet all was quiet. Evidently people were waiting intently for what came next; perhaps, in the silence, an outburst was gathering that would put an end to everything. It was annoying that the door at the far end of the hall now opened and the young washerwoman, who had probably finished her work, came in and, despite all the care she took, drew a few glances. Only the examining magistrate gave K. immediate satisfaction, for he seemed struck by the words at once. Until now he had listened standing, since K.'s address had caught him by surprise while he was on his feet addressing the gallery. Now, during the pause, he gradually sat down, as though hoping it would not be noticed. Probably to compose his expression, he took up the little notebook again.

“That won't help,” K. went on. “Your little notebook, too, Mr Examining Magistrate, confirms what I'm saying.” Satisfied to hear only his own calm words in this unfamiliar gathering, K. even dared to take the notebook from the examining magistrate without further ado and lift it by a middle page with his fingertips, as though shrinking from it, so that the closely written, stained, yellow-edged pages hung down on either side. “These are the examining magistrate's records,” he said, letting the notebook drop onto the table. “By all means go on reading it, Mr Examining Magistrate. I'm truly not afraid of this ledger of guilt, although it's inaccessible to me, since I can only touch it with two fingertips and cannot take it in my hand.” It could only be a sign of deep humiliation—or at least it had to be interpreted that way—that the examining magistrate reached for the notebook as it lay on the table, tried to put it somewhat in order, and took it up again to read.

The faces of the people in the front row were turned towards K. with such intentness that he looked down at them for a little while. They were all older men, some with white beards. Perhaps they were the ones who mattered, who could influence the whole gathering, which even the humiliation of the examining magistrate had not roused from the immobility into which it had sunk since K.'s speech began.

“What happened to me,” K. continued, a little more quietly than before, repeatedly searching the faces in the front row, which gave his speech a somewhat distracted air, “what happened to me is only an individual case, and as such not very important, since I don't take it too seriously. But it is a sign of proceedings such as are brought against many people. It is for them that I stand here, not for myself.”

He had raised his voice involuntarily. Somewhere someone clapped with upraised hands and shouted: “Bravo! Why not? Bravo! And bravo again!” Here and there the men in the front row reached into their beards; none turned round at the shout. K. attached no importance to it either, but was encouraged nevertheless. He no longer felt it necessary for everyone to applaud; it was enough if the gathering as a whole began thinking about the matter and only occasionally an individual was won over by persuasion.

“I don't want an orator's triumph,” K. said, following this train of thought. “It would probably be beyond my reach, anyway. The examining magistrate is probably a much better speaker; it's part of his profession, after all. All I want is a public discussion of a public abuse. Listen: I was arrested about ten days ago. I laugh at the fact of the arrest itself, but that's not relevant here. I was assaulted early in the morning in bed. Perhaps—judging by what the examining magistrate said, it can't be ruled out—they had orders to arrest some house painter just as innocent as I am, but they chose me. The adjoining room was occupied by two coarse guards. Had I been a dangerous robber, they could not have taken greater precautions. These guards were also a dissolute rabble. They talked my ears off; they wanted to be bribed; they wanted to wheedle my linen and clothes out of me under false pretences; they wanted money, supposedly to fetch me breakfast, after shamelessly eating my own breakfast before my eyes. Nor was that enough. I was taken into a third room before the supervisor. It was the room of a lady I hold in high regard, and I had to watch it being, in a sense, defiled by the presence of the guards and the supervisor, on my account but through no fault of mine. It was not easy to remain calm. But I managed it, and I asked the supervisor quite calmly—if he were here, he would have to confirm it—why I was under arrest. And what did this supervisor answer, whom I can still see before me, sitting in the lady's chair as the embodiment of the most obtuse arrogance? Gentlemen, in essence he answered nothing. Perhaps he really knew nothing; he had arrested me and was satisfied with that. He even went further and brought into this lady's room three junior employees of my bank, who occupied themselves with handling and disarranging photographs belonging to her. The presence of these employees naturally served another purpose too: like my landlady and her maid, they were to spread the news of my arrest, damage my public reputation and, in particular, undermine my position at the bank. Now, none of that succeeded, not in the slightest. Even my landlady, a very simple person—I want to mention her name here with honour; she is called Mrs Grubach—even Mrs Grubach had enough sense to see that an arrest like this meant no more than an attack carried out in the street by insufficiently supervised boys. I repeat: the whole affair has caused me only inconvenience and passing annoyance. But could it not have had worse consequences too?”

When K. paused here and looked towards the silent examining magistrate, he thought he noticed him just then signalling to someone in the crowd with a glance. K. smiled and said: “Here beside me, the examining magistrate is just giving one of you a secret signal. So there are people among you being directed from up here. I don't know whether that signal was supposed to produce hissing or applause, and by exposing the matter prematurely I am quite deliberately giving up the opportunity to learn what the signal means. It is a matter of complete indifference to me, and I publicly authorise the examining magistrate to command his paid employees down there in words spoken aloud, instead of with secret signals, saying, for example, one time: Now hiss, and the next: Now clap.”

The examining magistrate shifted back and forth in his chair, embarrassed or impatient. The man behind him, with whom he had been talking earlier, leaned towards him again, whether to encourage him in general or offer some particular advice. Below, people were talking quietly but animatedly. The two parties, which had earlier seemed to hold such opposite opinions, were mixing; some people pointed at K., others at the examining magistrate. The misty haze in the room was extremely trying; it even prevented a closer view of those standing farther away. It must have been particularly troublesome to the people in the gallery, who were forced, with timid sideways glances at the examining magistrate, to put quiet questions to the members of the gathering in order to learn more. The answers were given just as quietly, behind shielding hands.

“I'm nearly finished,” said K., banging his fist on the table because there was no bell. Startled by this, the heads of the examining magistrate and his adviser instantly flew apart. “I stand apart from this whole affair, so I can judge it calmly, and you may gain a great deal by listening to me, provided this supposed court matters to you at all. I ask you to postpone your discussions among yourselves of what I'm putting forward, because I have no time and shall soon leave.”

There was silence at once; K. already had that much command of the gathering. People were no longer shouting over one another as at the beginning; they were not even applauding any more, but they seemed convinced, or very nearly so.
