“There is no doubt,” K. said very quietly, pleased by the strained attention of the entire gathering; in this silence there arose a rushing sound more stirring than the most ecstatic applause, “there is no doubt that behind every manifestation of this court—in my case, then, behind the arrest and today's examination—stands a large organisation. An organisation that employs not only corruptible guards, foolish supervisors and examining magistrates who are mediocre at best, but also, certainly, maintains a judiciary of high and the highest ranks, with the countless, indispensable retinue of attendants, clerks, gendarmes and other assistants, perhaps even executioners—I don't shrink from the word. And the purpose of this large organisation, gentlemen? It consists in arresting innocent people and instituting senseless proceedings against them, usually, as in my case, without result. Given the senselessness of the whole thing, how could the worst corruption among the officials be concealed? It's impossible; even the highest judge could not manage that for himself alone. That is why the guards try to steal the clothes off arrested people's backs, why supervisors break into other people's homes, why the innocent are to be humiliated before entire gatherings rather than questioned. The guards merely told me about storerooms where the arrested people's property is taken. I'd like to see those storage places, where the possessions they have worked so hard to acquire are rotting, insofar as they haven't been stolen by thieving storeroom officials.”

K. was interrupted by a shriek from the far end of the hall. He shaded his eyes to see, because the dull daylight made the haze whitish and dazzling. It concerned the washerwoman, whom K. had recognised as a serious disturbance as soon as she entered. Whether she was now at fault or not could not be made out. K. saw only that a man had pulled her into a corner by the door and was pressing her against him there. But it was not she who was shrieking; it was the man. His mouth was stretched wide and he was looking at the ceiling. A small circle had formed around them; the people in the nearby gallery seemed delighted that the seriousness K. had introduced into the gathering had been interrupted in this way. His first impulse was to run over at once. He also thought everyone would want order restored there, and at least the couple removed from the hall, but the first rows in front of him remained solid; no one moved and no one let K. through. On the contrary, they obstructed him, and a hand—he had no time to turn round—seized him from behind by the collar. Old men held out their arms. K. was no longer really thinking of the couple; he felt as though his freedom were being restricted, as though they were making the arrest a serious matter, and he jumped down from the platform without regard for anyone. Now he stood eye to eye with the crowd. Had he misjudged these people? Had he expected too much effect from his speech? Had they been pretending while he spoke, and now that he was coming to his conclusions, were they tired of pretending? What faces surrounded him! Small black eyes darted back and forth; cheeks sagged like drunkards'; the long beards were stiff and sparse, and when hands reached into them, it seemed as though people were merely forming claws rather than grasping beards. But beneath the beards—and this was K.'s real discovery—badges of various sizes and colours gleamed on the coat collars. Everyone had these badges, as far as he could see. They all belonged together, the apparent parties on the right and left; and when he turned suddenly, he saw the same badges on the collar of the examining magistrate, who was looking calmly down with his hands in his lap. “So!” cried K., throwing his arms up; the sudden realisation demanded space. “You're all officials, I see. You're the corrupt gang I was speaking against. You've crowded in here as listeners and snoopers, pretended to form parties, and one of them applauded to test me. You wanted to learn how to lead innocent people astray. Well, I hope you've truly been here for nothing. Either you've amused yourselves at someone expecting you to defend innocence, or else—let go of me or I'll hit you!” K. shouted at a trembling old man who had pushed particularly close to him—“or else you've really learnt something. And with that I wish you luck in your trade.” He quickly took his hat, which lay on the edge of the table, and pushed towards the exit amid general silence, certainly the silence of utter surprise. But the examining magistrate seemed to have been even quicker than K., for he was waiting for him by the door. “One moment,” he said. K. stopped, but looked not at the examining magistrate, only at the door, whose handle he had already grasped. “I merely wanted to point out,” said the examining magistrate, “that today—you probably haven't realised it yet—you have deprived yourself of the advantage that questioning offers an arrested person in every case.” K. laughed at the door. “You scoundrels, you can keep all your questioning!” he shouted, opening the door and hurrying down the stairs. Behind him rose the noise of the gathering, lively once more, beginning to discuss the incidents in the manner of students.

chapters.title: Chapter 3
paragraphs: Throughout the following week K. waited from day to day for another notification. He could not believe they had taken his refusal to be questioned literally, and when the expected notification really had not arrived by Sunday evening, he assumed he had been summoned again, without its being said, to the same house at the same time. He therefore went there again on Sunday, this time making his way directly up the stairs and through the passages. Some people who remembered him greeted him at their doors, but he no longer had to ask anyone and soon reached the right door. It was opened as soon as he knocked, and without looking further at the woman he knew, who remained by the door, he was about to go straight into the adjoining room. “There is no sitting today,” said the woman. “Why shouldn't there be a sitting?” he asked, unwilling to believe it. But the woman convinced him by opening the door to the adjoining room. It was indeed empty, and in its emptiness looked even more miserable than it had the previous Sunday. Some books lay on the table, which stood unchanged on the platform. “May I look at the books?” K. asked, not out of any particular curiosity, but merely so as not to have come here for absolutely nothing. “No,” said the woman, closing the door again. “That isn't allowed. The books belong to the examining magistrate.” “Oh, I see,” said K., nodding. “The books are probably law books, and it is characteristic of this judicial system that people are condemned not only in innocence but also in ignorance.” “That must be so,” said the woman, who had not quite understood him. “Well, then I'll go,” said K. “Shall I give the examining magistrate a message?” asked the woman. “You know him?” K. asked. “Of course,” said the woman. “My husband is a court usher.” Only now did K. notice that the room which last time had contained only a washtub was now a fully furnished living room. The woman noticed his surprise and said: “Yes, we live here rent-free, but on days when the court sits we have to clear out the room. My husband's position has its disadvantages.” “I'm not so surprised by the room,” said K., looking at her angrily, “as by the fact that you're married.” “Perhaps you're referring to the incident at the last sitting, when I interrupted your speech?” asked the woman. “Of course,” said K. “It's over and almost forgotten now, but at the time it made me positively furious. And now you yourself tell me you're a married woman.” “It wasn't to your disadvantage that your speech was interrupted. People spoke very unfavourably about it afterwards.” “Perhaps,” said K., turning the subject aside, “but that doesn't excuse you.” “I'm excused by everyone who knows me,” said the woman. “The man who embraced me then has been pursuing me for a long time. I may not be generally attractive, but I am to him. There's no protection against it; even my husband has come to terms with it. If he wants to keep his position, he has to put up with it, because that man is a student and will probably rise to greater power. He's always after me; he left just before you arrived.” “It fits with everything else,” said K. “It doesn't surprise me.” “You want to improve a few things here, don't you?” the woman asked slowly and searchingly, as though saying something dangerous both to herself and to K. “I gathered that from your speech, which I personally liked very much. Admittedly, I heard only part of it; I missed the beginning, and during the end I was on the floor with the student.—It's so disgusting here,” she said after a pause, taking K.'s hand. “Do you think you'll manage to make things better?” K. smiled and turned his hand a little in her soft hands. “Actually,” he said, “I'm not employed to make things better here, as you put it, and if you said that to the examining magistrate, for example, you'd be laughed at or punished. In fact I certainly wouldn't have interfered in these matters of my own free will, and this judicial system's need for improvement would never have disturbed my sleep. But because I was supposedly arrested—I am under arrest, you see—I have been forced to intervene here, for my own sake. If in doing so I can be of any use to you as well, I shall of course be very glad. Not merely out of charity towards my neighbour, but also because you can help me too.” “How could I do that?” the woman asked. “By showing me, for instance, the books there on the table.” “Of course,” the woman exclaimed, hurriedly drawing him after her. They were old, worn books; one cover was almost broken in the middle, its pieces held together only by threads. “How dirty everything is here,” said K., shaking his head, and before he could reach for the books, the woman wiped away the dust with her apron, at least on the surface. K. opened the first book. An indecent picture appeared. A man and a woman sat naked on a sofa; the artist's vulgar intention was clear, but his ineptitude had been so great that in the end all one could see was a man and a woman sticking out of the picture with excessive bodily solidity, sitting much too upright and, owing to the faulty perspective, managing to turn towards one another only with difficulty. K. leafed no further, but merely opened the second book at its title page. It was a novel called “The Torments Grete Had to Endure from Her Husband Hans.” “These are the law books studied here,” said K. “These are the people who are to judge me.” “I'll help you,” said the woman. “Would you like that?” “Could you really do it without putting yourself in danger? You said just now that your husband was very dependent on his superiors.” “I'll help you nevertheless,” said the woman. “Come, we must discuss it. Don't speak about my danger any more. I fear danger only where I choose to fear it. Come.” She pointed to the platform and asked him to sit with her on the step. “You have beautiful dark eyes,” she said after they had sat down, looking up into K.'s face. “People tell me I have beautiful eyes too, but yours are much more beautiful. I noticed them immediately when you first came in here. They were also the reason I later came into the meeting room, which I never usually do and which is even, in a way, forbidden to me.” So that's all it is, K. thought. She's offering herself to me. She's corrupt like everyone else around here. She's tired of the court officials, which is understandable, and so welcomes any stranger at all with a compliment about his eyes. K. stood up without a word, as though he had spoken his thoughts aloud and thereby explained his behaviour to the woman. “I don't believe you could help me,” he said. “To help me really, you would need connections with senior officials. But you surely know only the lower employees who swarm about here. You certainly know them very well and could get quite a few things out of them, I don't doubt that; but the most you could obtain from them would be entirely irrelevant to the final outcome of the case. And in doing so you would still have lost a few friends. I don't want that. Carry on your previous relationship with these people; it seems to me that you can't do without it. I don't say that without regret, because, to return your compliment in some way, I find you attractive too, especially when you look at me so sadly, as you are now, though there's no reason for you to do so. You belong to the company I have to fight, but you're quite comfortable in it. You even love the student, and if you don't love him, you at least prefer him to your husband. That was easy to gather from what you said.” “No!” she exclaimed, remaining seated and merely reaching for K.'s hand, which he did not withdraw quickly enough. “You mustn't leave now. You mustn't leave with a false opinion of me. Could you really bring yourself to go now? Am I really so worthless that you won't even do me the favour of staying just a little longer?” “You misunderstand me,” said K., sitting down. “If it really matters to you that I stay, I'm happy to stay. I have time; I came expecting a hearing today. All I meant by what I said before was to ask you not to do anything for me in my case. But that needn't offend you either, when you consider that I don't care in the least how the case turns out and shall only laugh at a conviction. Assuming the case ever actually reaches a conclusion, which I very much doubt. I rather think the proceedings have already been discontinued, through laziness or forgetfulness, or perhaps even fear on the part of the officials, or will be discontinued before long. Of course, it's also possible that they'll pretend to carry the case on in the hope of some substantial bribe. Quite in vain, as I can tell them already, because I bribe no one. You could nevertheless do me a favour by telling the examining magistrate, or anyone else who likes spreading important news, that I shall never be induced to offer a bribe by any of the tricks of which these gentlemen undoubtedly have a rich supply. It would be quite hopeless; you can tell them that openly. But perhaps they've already noticed it themselves, and even if they haven't, I don't particularly care whether they find out now. It would only save the gentlemen work, and admittedly save me a few inconveniences, which I'm happy to take upon myself if I know that each one also strikes a blow at the others. And I intend to see that it does. Do you actually know the examining magistrate?” “Of course,” said the woman. “He was the very first person I thought of when I offered you help. I didn't know he was only a low-ranking official, but if you say so, it's probably true. Still, I believe the report he sends up has some influence. And he writes so many reports. You say the officials are lazy; certainly not all of them, especially not this examining magistrate. He writes a great deal. Last Sunday, for instance, the sitting went on until towards evening. Everyone left, but the examining magistrate stayed in the hall. I had to bring him a lamp. I had only a little kitchen lamp, but he was satisfied with it and began writing at once. Meanwhile my husband had come home too—he happened to have leave that Sunday—we fetched the furniture and put our room back in order; then some neighbours came, and we talked by a candle. In short, we forgot the examining magistrate and went to sleep. Suddenly, in the night—it must have been very late—I wake up, and the examining magistrate is standing beside the bed, shading the lamp with his hand so that no light falls on my husband. It was an unnecessary precaution: my husband sleeps so soundly that even the light wouldn't have woken him. I was so frightened I almost screamed, but the examining magistrate was very friendly, warned me to be careful, and whispered that he had been writing until now, that he was returning the lamp, and that he would never forget the sight of me as he had found me sleeping. All I meant to tell you by this is that the examining magistrate really does write a great many reports, especially about you, because your questioning was certainly one of the main subjects of the two-day sitting. Such long reports surely can't be entirely meaningless. Besides, you can also see from the incident that the examining magistrate is courting me and that just now, in these early days—he must only just have noticed me at all—I can have considerable influence over him. I now have other evidence, too, that I matter a great deal to him. Yesterday he sent me silk stockings as a present through the student, whom he trusts greatly and who works with him, supposedly for cleaning the courtroom; but that's only a pretext, since this work is simply my duty and my husband is paid for it. They're beautiful stockings, look”—she stretched her legs out, lifted her skirts to her knees and looked at the stockings herself—“they're beautiful stockings, but really too fine and unsuitable for me.”

Suddenly she broke off, laid her hand on K.'s as though to reassure him, and whispered: “Quiet, Bertold is watching us.” K. slowly raised his eyes. A young man stood in the doorway of the courtroom. He was short, his legs not quite straight, and sought to give himself dignity with a short, sparse, reddish full beard through which he continually ran his fingers. K. looked at him curiously: this was the first student of that unknown legal science whom he had, in a sense, encountered on a human footing, a man who would probably one day rise to higher official positions too. The student, on the other hand, apparently took no notice at all of K.; he merely beckoned to the woman with one finger, briefly withdrawn from his beard, and went to the window. The woman leaned towards K. and whispered: “Please don't be angry with me, I beg you, and don't think badly of me. I have to go to him now, to that horrible man. Just look at his crooked legs. But I'll come straight back, and then I'll go with you if you'll take me. I'll go wherever you want. You can do whatever you want with me. I'll be happy if I can get away from here for as long as possible, though I'd rather it were for ever.” She stroked K.'s hand once more, sprang up and ran to the window. Involuntarily K. still reached after her hand into empty air. The woman really did tempt him; despite all his thinking, he could find no sound reason not to yield to the temptation. He easily dismissed the fleeting objection that she might be trapping him for the court. How could she trap him? Did he not always remain free enough to smash the whole court at once, at least as far as it concerned him? Could he not have that small amount of confidence in himself? And her offer of help sounded sincere and might not be worthless. Perhaps, too, there could be no better revenge on the examining magistrate and his followers than to take this woman away from them and claim her for himself. It might then happen one night that, after laboriously composing lying reports about K., the examining magistrate found the woman's bed empty. Empty because she belonged to K., because this woman at the window, this voluptuous, supple, warm body in a dark dress of coarse, heavy fabric, belonged entirely and solely to K.

Having disposed of his misgivings about the woman in this way, he found the quiet conversation at the window too long. He tapped the platform with his knuckles and then with his fist. The student glanced briefly at K. over the woman's shoulder but would not be disturbed; indeed, he pressed closer to her and put his arms around her. She lowered her head deeply, as though listening attentively to him; as she bent, he kissed her loudly on the neck without substantially interrupting his speech. K. saw this as confirmation of the tyranny the student exercised over her, according to her complaints. He stood up and walked about the room. Glancing sideways at the student, he considered how to get rid of him as quickly as possible, and so was not displeased when the student, evidently disturbed by K.'s walking, which had at times turned into stamping, remarked: “If you're impatient, you can leave. You could have left before now. No one would have missed you. Indeed, you should have left, as soon as I came in, and as quickly as possible.” All manner of rage might have erupted in that remark, but in any case it also contained the arrogance of a future court official speaking to an unwelcome defendant. K. stopped very close to him and said with a smile: “I am impatient, that's true, but that impatience would be most easily removed if you left us. If, however, you've come here to study—I heard that you're a student—I'll gladly make room for you and leave with the woman. Besides, you'll have a great deal more studying to do before you become a judge. Admittedly I don't yet know your judicial system very well, but I assume that coarse talk alone, which you already command with shameless skill, is nowhere near enough.” “He shouldn't have been allowed to roam around so freely,” the student said, as though explaining K.'s insulting speech to the woman. “It was a mistake. I told the examining magistrate so. They should at least have kept him in his room between questionings. The examining magistrate is sometimes incomprehensible.” “Useless talk,” said K., reaching for the woman. “Come.” “Oh, I see,” said the student. “No, no, you're not getting her.” And with a strength no one would have expected of him, he lifted her onto one arm and ran towards the door with his back bent, looking up at her tenderly. A certain fear of K. was unmistakable, yet he still dared to provoke him by stroking and squeezing the woman's arm with his free hand. K. ran alongside him for a few paces, ready to seize him and, if necessary, throttle him, when the woman said: “It's no use. The examining magistrate has sent for me. I can't go with you. This little monster”—here she passed her hand over the student's face—“this little monster won't let me.” “And you don't want to be freed!” K. shouted, laying his hand on the shoulder of the student, who snapped at it with his teeth. “No!” the woman cried, warding K. off with both hands. “No, no, anything but that! What are you thinking of? It would ruin me. Leave him alone, please, leave him alone. He's only carrying out the examining magistrate's order and taking me to him.” “Then let him run, and I never want to see you again,” said K., furious with disappointment, giving the student a push in the back that made him stumble briefly, only to spring all the higher with his burden a moment later, delighted that he had not fallen. K. followed them slowly, recognising that this was the first unmistakable defeat these people had inflicted on him. There was, of course, no reason to be afraid on that account; he had suffered the defeat only because he had sought the fight. If he stayed at home and led his usual life, he was a thousand times superior to any of these people and could kick any of them out of his way. And he imagined the most ridiculous scene possible, if, for example, this wretched student, this puffed-up child, this crooked, bearded creature knelt beside Elsa's bed and begged for mercy with folded hands. K. liked the picture so much that he resolved to take the student along to Elsa's one day, if any opportunity at all presented itself.

Out of curiosity K. hurried to the door as well. He wanted to see where the woman was being carried; surely the student would not carry her through the streets in his arms. The journey proved much shorter. Directly opposite the apartment door a narrow wooden staircase led probably to the attic; it turned, so that its end could not be seen. The student carried the woman up these stairs, now very slowly and groaning, for his running so far had weakened him. The woman waved down to K. and tried, by raising and lowering her shoulders, to show that she was not to blame for being carried off, though there was not much regret in the movement. K. looked at her without expression, as at a stranger. He wanted to reveal neither that he was disappointed nor that he could easily overcome his disappointment.

The two had already disappeared, but K. was still standing in the doorway. He had to assume that the woman had not only betrayed him but lied to him as well when she said she was being carried to the examining magistrate. Surely the examining magistrate would not be sitting in the attic waiting. However long one looked at it, the wooden staircase explained nothing. Then K. noticed a little notice beside the stairs, went over and read, in a childish, unpractised hand: “Stairs to the court offices.” So the court offices were here, in the attic of this tenement? This was not an arrangement capable of inspiring much respect, and it was reassuring for an accused man to imagine how little money this court had at its disposal if it housed its offices where the tenants, already among the poorest people themselves, threw their useless rubbish. Admittedly, it was possible that there was money enough, but the officials fell upon it before it could be used for court purposes. In light of K.'s experience so far, that was even very likely; in that case, however, such degradation of the court, though humiliating for an accused man, was fundamentally even more reassuring than the court's poverty would have been. Now K. also understood why, at the first questioning, they had been ashamed to summon the accused to an attic and had preferred to trouble him in his own home. What a position K. occupied in relation to the judge sitting in the attic, when he himself had a large room with an anteroom at the bank and could look through an enormous window down onto the busy city square. Admittedly, he had no additional income from bribes or embezzlement, nor could he have an attendant carry a woman into his office in his arms. But K. was quite happy to forgo that, at least in this life.

K. was still standing in front of the notice when a man came up the stairs, looked through the open door into the living room, from which the courtroom could also be seen, and finally asked K. whether he had seen a woman here a short while before. “You're the court usher, aren't you?” asked K. “Yes,” said the man. “Oh, you're the accused man K. Now I recognise you too. Welcome.” And he held out his hand to K., who had not expected it at all. “But no sitting has been announced for today,” the court usher then said, as K. remained silent. “I know,” said K., examining the usher's civilian coat, whose only official insignia were two gilded buttons among some ordinary ones; they seemed to have been cut off an old officer's greatcoat. “I spoke to your wife a little while ago. She's no longer here. The student carried her to the examining magistrate.” “You see,” said the court usher, “they're always carrying her away from me. Today is Sunday, and I'm under no obligation to work, but just to get me away from here they send me off with a useless message. And they don't send me far, so I can hope that if I hurry very much I may still get back in time. So I run as fast as I can, shout my message through the gap in the door of the office I've been sent to, so breathlessly that they can scarcely have understood it, and run back again. But the student has hurried even more than I have, though admittedly he had a shorter way to go; he only had to run down the attic stairs. If I weren't so dependent, I'd have crushed the student against this wall long ago. Here beside the notice. I dream of it all the time. Here, a little above the floor, he's pinned fast, arms stretched out, fingers spread, crooked legs twisted into a circle, and blood spattered all around. But so far it's only been a dream.” “Is there no other remedy?” K. asked with a smile. “I don't know of one,” said the court usher. “And now it's getting worse. Until now he only carried her off to his own place; now, as I had long expected, he carries her to the examining magistrate as well.” “Is your wife entirely blameless in this?” K. asked. He had to control himself as he asked, so strongly did he too now feel jealousy. “Oh, certainly not,” said the court usher. “She's the most to blame. She attached herself to him. As for him, he runs after every woman. In this house alone he's already been thrown out of five apartments he slipped into. My wife is the most beautiful woman in the whole house, of course, and I'm precisely the one who isn't allowed to defend himself.” “If that's how things stand, then there really is no remedy,” said K. “Why not?” asked the court usher. “The student is a coward. Someone would have to thrash him just once, when he tries to touch my wife, so thoroughly that he never dares again. But I'm not allowed to, and other people won't do me the favour because they're all afraid of his power. Only a man like you could do it.” “Why me?” K. asked in astonishment. “You're accused, after all,” said the court usher. “Yes,” said K., “but all the more reason for me to fear that, even if he perhaps has no influence on the outcome of the case, he probably has some over the preliminary investigation.” “Yes, certainly,” said the court usher, as though K.'s view were exactly as correct as his own. “But as a rule we don't conduct hopeless cases here.” “I don't agree with you,” said K., “but that won't stop me from giving the student some attention when the opportunity arises.” “I'd be very grateful,” said the court usher somewhat formally; it seemed that he did not really believe his greatest wish could be fulfilled. “Perhaps,” K. continued, “some of your other officials, perhaps even all of them, deserve the same.” “Yes, yes,” said the court usher, as though this went without saying. Then he gave K. a trusting look, unlike any he had given him so far despite all his friendliness, and added: “One is always rebelling, after all.” But the conversation seemed to have become a little uncomfortable for him, for he broke it off, saying: “Now I have to report to the office. Would you like to come?” “I have no business there,” said K. “You could look at the offices. No one will pay any attention to you.” “Are they worth seeing?” K. asked hesitantly, though very eager to go along. “Well,” said the court usher, “I thought you might be interested.” “All right,” K. said at last. “I'll come.” And he ran up the stairs faster than the court usher.

He almost fell as he entered, for there was another step behind the door. “They don't show much consideration for the public,” he said. “They show no consideration at all,” said the court usher. “Just look at the waiting room here.” It was a long corridor from which roughly made wooden doors led into the separate compartments of the attic. Although no light entered directly, it was not completely dark, for some compartments had, instead of solid plank walls facing the corridor, mere wooden gratings, extending all the way to the ceiling, through which some light passed and through which individual officials could also be seen writing at desks or standing right at the gratings, watching the people in the corridor through the gaps. There were only a few people in the corridor, probably because it was Sunday. They gave a very humble impression. They sat at almost regular distances from one another on two rows of long wooden benches set along either side. All were shabbily dressed, although most, judging by their expressions, bearing, style of beard and many small details that could scarcely be pinned down, belonged to the higher classes. Since there were no coat hooks, they had put their hats under the benches, probably following one another's example. When those sitting nearest the door saw K. and the court usher, they stood up in greeting; seeing this, those farther along thought they too must greet them, so everyone rose as the two passed. They never stood fully upright: backs bent, knees buckled, they stood like beggars in the street. K. waited for the court usher, who was walking a little behind him, and said: “How humiliated they must be.” “Yes,” said the court usher. “They're accused people. Everyone you see here is accused.” “Really!” said K. “Then they're my colleagues.” He turned to the nearest, a tall, slim man whose hair was already almost grey. “What are you waiting for here?” K. asked politely. But being addressed unexpectedly confused the man, which looked all the more painful because he was evidently a man of the world who elsewhere certainly knew how to control himself and did not easily surrender the superiority he had acquired over many people. Here, however, he could not answer so simple a question and looked at the others as though they were obliged to help him, and as though no one could demand an answer from him if that help failed to come. The court usher stepped forward and said, to reassure and encourage him: “The gentleman is only asking what you're waiting for. Do answer.” The usher's voice, probably familiar to him, had a better effect. “I'm waiting—” he began, then faltered. Evidently he had chosen this beginning to answer the question exactly as it had been put, but now could find no continuation. Some of those waiting had come closer and were standing around the group. The usher said to them: “Away, away, keep the corridor clear.” They moved back a little, but not as far as their former seats. Meanwhile the man who had been questioned had collected himself and even answered with a small smile: “A month ago I made some applications for evidence to be taken in my case, and I'm waiting for them to be dealt with.” “You seem to be taking a great deal of trouble,” said K. “Yes,” said the man, “it is my case, after all.” “Not everyone thinks as you do,” said K. “I, for example, am accused too, but as I hope for salvation, I have neither applied for evidence to be taken nor done anything else of the sort. Do you consider it necessary?” “I don't know exactly,” said the man, once more utterly uncertain. Evidently he thought K. was joking with him, and for fear of making some new mistake he would probably have preferred to repeat his earlier answer in full; but faced with K.'s impatient look, he merely said: “For my part, I have applied for evidence to be taken.” “You don't believe I'm accused, do you?” K. asked. “Oh, please, certainly,” said the man, stepping a little aside, but there was no belief in the answer, only fear. “So you don't believe me?” K. asked, taking him by the arm, unconsciously prompted by the man's humility, as though to force him to believe. He did not mean to hurt him, and had only touched him very lightly, yet the man cried out as though K. had seized him not with two fingers but with red-hot pincers. This ridiculous crying finally exhausted K.'s patience. If they did not believe he was accused, so much the better; perhaps the man even took him for a judge. Now, in parting, he really did grip him more firmly, pushed him back onto the bench and went on. “Most accused people are so sensitive,” said the court usher. Behind them almost everyone waiting now gathered around the man, who had already stopped crying out, and seemed to be questioning him closely about the incident. A guard now approached K., identifiable chiefly by a sabre whose scabbard, judging at least by its colour, was aluminium. K. marvelled at it and even reached out to touch it. The guard, who had come because of the shouting, asked what had happened. The court usher tried to reassure him in a few words, but the guard declared that he must nevertheless go and see for himself, saluted and went on with very hurried but very short steps, probably measured out by gout.

K. did not concern himself for long with the guard or the people in the corridor, particularly since, about halfway along it, he saw an opportunity to turn right through an opening without a door. He checked with the court usher that this was the right way; the usher nodded, and K. duly turned in. He found it unpleasant that he always had to walk one or two paces ahead of the usher; in this place, at least, it could give the impression that he was being brought in under arrest. So he often waited for the usher, but the man immediately fell behind again. Finally, to put an end to his discomfort, K. said: “Now I've seen what it's like here. I want to leave.” “You haven't seen everything yet,” said the court usher quite innocently. “I don't want to see everything,” said K., who in fact felt tired. “I want to go. How do I get to the exit?” “Surely you haven't lost your way already?” the court usher asked in surprise. “Go to the corner here, then right along the corridor, straight to the door.” “Come with me,” said K. “Show me the way. I'll miss it; there are so many passages here.” “It's the only way,” said the court usher, now reproachfully. “I can't go back with you again. I have to deliver my report, and I've already lost a great deal of time because of you.” “Come with me,” K. repeated more sharply now, as though he had finally caught the usher in a lie. “Please don't shout so,” the usher whispered. “There are offices everywhere here. If you don't want to go back alone, come a little farther with me or wait here until I've delivered my report, and then I'll gladly go back with you.” “No, no,” said K. “I won't wait, and you must come with me now.” K. had not yet looked around the space where he stood; only now, when one of the many wooden doors surrounding it opened, did he look over. A girl, probably drawn by K.'s loud talking, came in and asked: “What does the gentleman want?” Behind her, in the distance, a man could also be seen approaching through the half-dark. K. looked at the court usher. He had said no one would pay attention to K., and now two people were already coming. It would take very little for the officials to notice him and demand an explanation for his presence. The only comprehensible and acceptable one was that he was an accused man who wanted to find out the date of his next questioning, but that was precisely the explanation he did not want to give, particularly since it was not truthful either: he had come only out of curiosity or, what was still less possible as an explanation, from a desire to establish that the interior of this judicial system was as repulsive as its exterior. And it did seem that he had been right in that assumption. He did not want to penetrate any farther; he felt oppressed enough by what he had seen so far. Just now he was in no state to face a senior official, who might appear from behind any door. He wanted to leave, with the court usher, or alone if he had to.

But standing there in silence must have made him conspicuous, and indeed the girl and the court usher looked at him as though some great transformation were bound to overtake him in the next minute and they did not want to miss seeing it. In the doorway stood the man K. had earlier noticed in the distance, holding on to the lintel of the low door and rocking a little on his toes like an impatient spectator. The girl, however, was the first to recognise that K.'s behaviour arose from a slight indisposition. She brought a chair and asked: “Wouldn't you like to sit down?” K. sat at once and, to gain better support, rested his elbows on the arms. “You're a little dizzy, aren't you?” she asked. Her face was now close in front of him; it had the stern expression some women have precisely in the finest bloom of their youth. “Don't worry about it,” she said. “It's nothing unusual here. Almost everyone has an attack like that the first time they come. Is this your first time here? Well, yes, but it's nothing unusual. The sun beats down on the roof timbers, and the hot wood makes the air so close and heavy. That's why the place isn't very suitable for offices, whatever great advantages it offers in other respects. But as for the air, on days when a lot of people come on business—and that's almost every day—it's scarcely breathable. If you also consider that washing is often hung up here to dry—we can't entirely forbid the tenants to do it—you won't be surprised any more that you felt a little ill. But in the end you get quite used to the air. When you come for the second or third time, you'll hardly feel how oppressive it is here. Are you feeling better already?” K. did not answer. It was too humiliating to find himself at these people's mercy through this sudden weakness; besides, now that he had learnt the causes of his nausea, he felt not better but a little worse. The girl noticed at once and, to give K. some fresh air, took a hooked pole leaning against the wall and pushed open a small hatch directly above him that led outside. But so much soot fell in that she immediately had to close the hatch again and wipe the soot from K.'s hands with her handkerchief, since he was too tired to do it himself. He would gladly have remained sitting quietly until he had recovered enough strength to leave, and that was bound to happen sooner the less attention people paid to him. But now the girl also said: “You can't stay here; we're blocking the traffic.” K. asked with his eyes what traffic he could possibly be blocking here. “If you like, I'll take you to the sickroom.” “Please help me,” she said to the man in the doorway, who immediately came closer. But K. did not want to go to the sickroom; being led farther in was precisely what he wanted to avoid. The farther he went, the worse it was bound to become. “I can walk now,” he therefore said, and rose trembling, having been spoiled by sitting comfortably. But then he could not hold himself upright. “It won't work after all,” he said, shaking his head, and sat down again with a sigh. He remembered the court usher, who despite everything could easily lead him out, but the usher seemed to have gone long ago. K. looked between the girl and the man standing before him, but could not find him.

“I think,” said the man, who incidentally was elegantly dressed and particularly noticeable for a grey waistcoat ending in two long, sharply cut points, “the gentleman's indisposition is due to the atmosphere here. It would therefore be best, and would suit him best too, if we took him not to the sickroom but out of the offices altogether.” “That's it!” K. cried, almost interrupting the man in his joy. “I'll certainly feel better at once. I'm not so weak, either; I only need a little support under the arms. I won't give you much trouble, and it isn't far. Just take me to the door; then I'll sit on the steps a little longer and soon recover. I don't suffer from attacks like this at all, you see; I'm surprised myself. I'm an office worker too, and accustomed to office air, but it seems altogether too much here, as you say yourselves. So would you be kind enough to guide me a little? I'm dizzy, you see, and I feel sick when I stand up on my own.” He raised his shoulders to make it easier for them both to take him under the arms.

But the man did not respond to the request. He kept his hands in his trouser pockets and laughed loudly. “You see,” he said to the girl, “I was right after all. The gentleman only feels ill here, not in general.” The girl smiled too, but lightly tapped the man's arm with her fingertips, as though he had carried his joke with K. too far. “But what are you thinking?” the man said, still laughing. “I really do intend to take the gentleman out.” “Then that's all right,” said the girl, briefly bowing her delicate head. “Don't attach too much importance to the laughter,” she said to K., who had grown sad again and was staring ahead, apparently needing no explanation. “This gentleman—may I introduce you?” The gentleman gave permission with a gesture. “This gentleman is the information officer. He gives the people waiting all the information they need, and since our judicial system isn't very well known among the public, a great deal of information is wanted. He has an answer to every question; you can test him on that if you ever feel like it. But that isn't his only merit. His second merit is his elegant clothing. We—that is, the staff—once thought that the information officer, who deals with people constantly and is their first point of contact, should also be elegantly dressed, for the sake of a dignified first impression. The rest of us, as you can see from me, are unfortunately very badly and old-fashionedly dressed. There's not much point in spending anything on clothes, either, since we're almost constantly in the offices; we even sleep here. But as I said, we once considered good clothes necessary for the information officer. Since our administration, which is a little peculiar in this respect, wouldn't provide them, we took up a collection—people with business here contributed too—and bought him this fine suit and some others. Everything would now be ready to make a good impression, but he ruins it again with his laughter and frightens people.” “That's how it is,” the gentleman said mockingly. “But I don't understand, miss, why you're telling the gentleman all our private affairs, or rather forcing them on him, since he doesn't want to hear them at all. Just look at him sitting there, evidently occupied with his own concerns.” K. did not even feel like disagreeing. The girl's intention might be good; perhaps she meant to distract him or give him a chance to collect himself, but she had chosen the wrong means. “I had to explain your laughter to him,” the girl said. “It was insulting.” “I think he'd forgive even worse insults if I eventually took him out.” K. said nothing and did not even look up. He allowed the two to discuss him as though he were an object; indeed, he preferred it that way. But suddenly he felt the information officer's hand on one arm and the girl's hand on the other. “Up you get, then, you weak man,” said the information officer. “Thank you both very much,” K. said, pleasantly surprised, slowly getting up and guiding their hands himself to the places where he most needed support. “It looks,” the girl said quietly into K.'s ear as they approached the corridor, “as though I'm particularly anxious to show the information officer in a good light, but let people think that; I still want to tell the truth. He hasn't a hard heart. He's not obliged to lead sick people out, yet he does it, as you see. Perhaps none of us is hard-hearted; perhaps we'd all gladly help. But as court officials we easily give the impression of being hard-hearted and unwilling to help anyone. I positively suffer from it.” “Wouldn't you like to sit down here for a little?” asked the information officer. They were already in the corridor, directly in front of the accused man K. had spoken to earlier. K. almost felt ashamed before him. Earlier he had stood so upright in front of him; now he had to be supported by two people. The information officer balanced his hat on spread fingers; his hair was disordered and hung over his sweat-covered forehead. But the accused man seemed to notice none of this. He stood humbly before the information officer, who looked over his head, and sought only to excuse his presence. “I know,” he said, “that a decision on my applications can't be given today. But I came anyway. I thought I could wait here. It's Sunday, I have time, and I'm not disturbing anyone here.” “You needn't make so many excuses,” said the information officer. “Your diligence is quite commendable. You are taking up space here unnecessarily, but nevertheless, as long as it doesn't become a nuisance to me, I certainly won't prevent you from following the progress of your case closely. When one has seen people disgracefully neglect their duty, one learns to be patient with people like you. Sit down.” “How well he knows how to speak to people,” the girl whispered. K. nodded, but started immediately when the information officer again asked him: “Wouldn't you like to sit down here?” “No,” said K. “I don't want to rest.” He had said it as firmly as possible, though in reality sitting down would have done him a great deal of good. He felt seasick. He thought he was on a ship in heavy seas. It seemed to him that water was crashing against the wooden walls, that a roar like breaking water came from the depths of the corridor, that the corridor was rocking sideways and the people waiting were being lowered and raised on either side. All the more incomprehensible was the calmness of the girl and the man guiding him. He was at their mercy; if they let go, he would fall like a plank. Sharp glances darted back and forth from their little eyes. K. felt their even steps without taking them himself, for he was almost carried from step to step. At last he noticed that they were speaking to him, but did not understand them; he heard only the noise filling everything, through which a constant high note seemed to sound like a siren. “Louder,” he whispered with his head lowered, ashamed, for he knew they had spoken loudly enough, though he could not understand them. Then at last, as though the wall before them had been torn open, a breath of fresh air came towards him, and he heard someone beside him say: “First he wants to leave, and then you can tell him a hundred times that this is the exit and he doesn't move.” K. realised he was standing in front of the exit door, which the girl had opened. He felt as though all his strength had returned at once. To get a foretaste of freedom, he immediately stepped onto a stair and took leave of his companions from there as they bent down towards him. “Thank you very much,” he repeated, shaking both their hands again and again, stopping only when he thought he saw that, accustomed to the office air, they could not bear the comparatively fresh air coming up the stairs. They could scarcely answer, and the girl might have fallen if K. had not closed the door extremely quickly. He then stood still for another moment, smoothed his hair with the help of a pocket mirror, picked up his hat, which lay on the next landing—the information officer had probably thrown it there—and ran down the stairs so freshly and in such long leaps that the change almost frightened him. His otherwise thoroughly stable health had never given him such surprises before. Was his body trying to revolt and prepare a new trial for him, since he bore the old one so effortlessly? He did not entirely dismiss the idea of seeing a doctor at the next opportunity. In any case, though—and on this he could advise himself—he intended to use every future Sunday morning better than this one.

chapters.title: Chapter 4
paragraphs: For some time afterwards K. found it impossible to exchange even a few words with Miss Bürstner. He tried in all sorts of ways to approach her, but she always knew how to prevent it. He came home immediately after work, sat on the sofa in his room without turning on the light, and occupied himself with nothing but watching the entrance hall. If the maid happened to pass and closed the door of the apparently empty room, he got up after a little while and opened it again. In the mornings he rose an hour earlier than usual in the hope of meeting Miss Bürstner alone as she went to her office. But none of these attempts succeeded. Then he wrote her a letter, both to her office and to the apartment, in which he again sought to justify his behaviour, offered any form of redress, promised never to overstep whatever boundaries she set him, and asked only to be given the opportunity of speaking to her once, particularly since he could make no arrangements with Mrs Grubach until he had first consulted her. Finally he told her that the following Sunday he would wait in his room all day for some sign from her that offered the prospect of his request being granted, or at least explained why she could not grant it although he had promised to defer to her in everything. The letters were not returned, but no answer came either. On Sunday, however, there was a sign clear enough. Early in the morning K. noticed through the keyhole unusual activity in the entrance hall, which was soon explained. A teacher of French—she was in fact German and called Montag—a frail, pale young woman with a slight limp, who had until now occupied a room of her own, was moving into Miss Bürstner's room. For hours she could be seen shuffling through the entrance hall. There was always another piece of linen, a little cloth or a book that had been forgotten and had to be fetched specially and carried to the new accommodation.

When Mrs Grubach brought K. his breakfast—since she had angered him so much, she no longer left even the slightest service to the maid—he could not restrain himself from speaking to her for the first time. “Why is there such a noise in the entrance hall today?” he asked while pouring the coffee. “Couldn't it be stopped? Must the tidying be done on a Sunday?” Although K. did not look up at Mrs Grubach, he noticed her breathe as though in relief. Even these stern questions she took as forgiveness or the beginning of forgiveness. “There's no tidying going on, Mr K.,” she said. “Miss Montag is only moving in with Miss Bürstner and carrying her things over.” She said nothing more, but waited to see how K. would take it and whether he would allow her to go on. K., however, put her to the test, thoughtfully stirring his coffee with the spoon and remaining silent. Then he looked up at her and said: “Have you given up your earlier suspicions about Miss Bürstner yet?” “Mr K.!” exclaimed Mrs Grubach, who had been waiting only for this question, holding her clasped hands out towards him. “You took a casual remark so much to heart the other day. I never remotely intended to offend you or anyone else. You've known me long enough, Mr K., to be sure of that. You've no idea how I've suffered these last few days! Me, slander my lodgers! And you believed it, Mr K.! And you said I should give you notice! Give you notice!” The last cry was already choked with tears. She raised her apron to her face and sobbed aloud.

“Please don't cry, Mrs Grubach,” said K., looking out of the window. He was thinking only of Miss Bürstner and of her having taken another girl into her room. “Please don't cry,” he said again when he turned back into the room and Mrs Grubach was still crying. “I didn't mean it so badly then either. We simply misunderstood each other. That can happen even between old friends.” Mrs Grubach lowered her apron below her eyes to see whether K. was really reconciled. “Yes, that's how it is,” said K., and now, since her behaviour suggested that the captain had revealed nothing, he ventured to add: “Do you really think I could quarrel with you over a girl I hardly know?” “That's precisely it, Mr K.,” said Mrs Grubach. It was her misfortune that as soon as she felt at all freer she immediately said something clumsy. “I kept asking myself: Why does Mr K. take Miss Bürstner's side so strongly? Why does he quarrel with me over her, although he knows that every angry word from him robs me of sleep? After all, I've said nothing about the young lady except what I've seen with my own eyes.” K. said nothing to this; with his first word he would have had to drive her from the room, and he did not want to. He contented himself with drinking his coffee and making Mrs Grubach feel that she was superfluous. Outside they could again hear Miss Montag's dragging steps as she crossed the entire entrance hall. “Do you hear that?” K. asked, gesturing towards the door. “Yes,” said Mrs Grubach with a sigh. “I wanted to help her and have the maid help too, but she's stubborn; she wants to move everything herself. I'm surprised at Miss Bürstner. I often find it trying enough to have Miss Montag as a lodger, but Miss Bürstner is even taking her into her room.” “That needn't concern you at all,” said K., crushing the remaining sugar in his cup. “Does it cause you any loss?” “No,” said Mrs Grubach. “In itself it's quite welcome to me; it frees a room where I can put my nephew, the captain. I've been afraid for some time that he might have disturbed you these past few days, while I've had to let him stay next door in the living room. He isn't very considerate.” “What ideas you have!” said K., standing up. “There's no question of that. You seem to think I'm oversensitive because I can't endure these wanderings of Miss Montag's—there she goes back again.” Mrs Grubach felt quite powerless. “Shall I tell her to put off the rest of the move, Mr K.? If you wish, I'll do it at once.” “But she's supposed to move in with Miss Bürstner!” said K. “Yes,” said Mrs Grubach, not quite understanding what he meant. “Well, then,” said K., “she has to carry her things over.” Mrs Grubach merely nodded. This silent helplessness, outwardly indistinguishable from defiance, irritated K. still more. He began pacing between the window and the door, thereby depriving Mrs Grubach of the opportunity to leave, which she would otherwise probably have done.

K. had just reached the door again when there was a knock. It was the maid, reporting that Miss Montag would like a few words with Mr K. and therefore asked him to come to the dining room, where she was waiting. K. listened thoughtfully to the maid, then turned an almost mocking look on the startled Mrs Grubach. The look seemed to say that he had long foreseen this invitation from Miss Montag and that it fitted perfectly with the torment he was being made to endure that Sunday morning by Mrs Grubach's lodgers. He sent the maid back with the answer that he would come at once, then went to the wardrobe to change his jacket. In response to Mrs Grubach, who was quietly lamenting the troublesome woman, he merely asked her to take the breakfast things away. “But you've hardly touched anything,” said Mrs Grubach. “Oh, do take it away!” K. cried. He felt as though Miss Montag were somehow mixed into everything, making it repulsive.
As he crossed the entrance hall, he looked towards the closed door of Miss Bürstner's room. But he had not been invited there, only to the dining room, whose door he pulled open without knocking.

It was a very long but narrow room with one window. There was only enough space for two cupboards to stand at angles in the corners beside the door; all the rest was taken up by the long dining table, which began near the door and reached almost to the large window, making it virtually inaccessible. The table was already laid for a great many people, since almost all the lodgers ate their midday meal here on Sundays.

When K. came in, Miss Montag approached from the window along one side of the table. They greeted each other silently. Then Miss Montag, holding her head unusually high as always, said: “I don't know whether you know me.” K. looked at her with narrowed eyes. “Certainly,” he said. “You've been living with Mrs Grubach for quite some time.” “But I believe you don't take much interest in the boarding house,” said Miss Montag. “No,” said K. “Won't you sit down?” said Miss Montag. In silence they each drew out a chair at the far end of the table and sat facing one another. But Miss Montag immediately got up again, for she had left her handbag on the windowsill, and went to fetch it, dragging her way across the whole room. When she returned, lightly swinging the handbag, she said: “I only want to speak a few words to you on behalf of my friend. She wanted to come herself, but she's feeling a little unwell today. She asks you to excuse her and hear me in her place. She couldn't have told you anything different from what I shall tell you. On the contrary, I believe I can tell you even more, since I'm comparatively uninvolved. Don't you agree?”

“What is there to say?” replied K., tired of seeing Miss Montag's eyes constantly fixed on his lips. In this way she was already claiming authority over what he had yet to say. “Miss Bürstner evidently doesn't wish to grant me the private conversation I asked her for.” “That's it,” said Miss Montag, “or rather, that isn't it at all. You put it with peculiar sharpness. Generally speaking, conversations are neither granted nor refused. But people may consider a conversation unnecessary, and that is what has happened here. Now, after your remark, I can speak openly. You asked my friend, in writing or in person, for a conversation. My friend, however, knows—or so I must assume—what that conversation would concern, and for reasons I don't know she is therefore convinced that no one would benefit if it actually took place. Besides, she only told me about it yesterday and very briefly. She said then that it couldn't matter very much to you either, since the idea had occurred to you only by chance, and you would realise for yourself, without any special explanation, if not already then very soon, how pointless the whole thing was. I replied that that might be true, but that for complete clarity I would nevertheless consider it useful to send you an explicit answer. I offered to undertake the task, and after some hesitation my friend gave in to me. Now I hope I have acted in your interests too, because even the smallest uncertainty in the most trivial matter is always distressing, and if, as in this case, it can easily be removed, surely it is better to do so at once.” “Thank you,” K. said immediately, slowly standing up, looking at Miss Montag, then across the table, then out of the window—the house opposite stood in sunlight—and going towards the door. Miss Montag followed him a few paces, as though she did not quite trust him. But at the door both had to step back, for it opened and Captain Lanz entered. K. saw him close up for the first time. He was a tall man of about forty, with a sunburnt, fleshy face. He made a slight bow that included K., then went to Miss Montag and respectfully kissed her hand. His movements were very assured. His courtesy towards Miss Montag contrasted strikingly with K.'s treatment of her. Nevertheless, Miss Montag did not seem angry with K.; indeed, as K. thought he noticed, she even wanted to introduce him to the captain. But K. did not want to be introduced. He would have been incapable of showing any friendliness either to the captain or to Miss Montag. The kiss on her hand had joined them, in his eyes, into a group intent on keeping him away from Miss Bürstner under an appearance of the greatest innocence and selflessness. Yet K. believed he understood not only that; he also understood that Miss Montag had chosen a good, though double-edged, method. She exaggerated the importance of the relationship between Miss Bürstner and K., above all the importance of the requested conversation, while trying at the same time to make it seem that K. was the one exaggerating everything. She would be proved wrong. K. intended to exaggerate nothing; he knew that Miss Bürstner was a little typist who should not resist him for long. In this he deliberately took no account at all of what he had learnt about her from Mrs Grubach. He considered all this as he left the room with scarcely a farewell. He meant to go straight to his own room, but a small laugh from Miss Montag, which he heard behind him from the dining room, gave him the idea that perhaps he could surprise both her and the captain. He looked around and listened for any disturbance that might come from the surrounding rooms. All was quiet; only the conversation in the dining room could be heard, and Mrs Grubach's voice from the passage leading to the kitchen. The opportunity seemed favourable. K. went to Miss Bürstner's door and knocked softly. When nothing stirred, he knocked again, but still no answer came. Was she asleep? Or really unwell? Or was she merely pretending not to be there because she guessed that only K. could be knocking so softly? K. assumed she was pretending and knocked harder. Finally, since the knocking had no effect, he opened the door cautiously, not without the feeling that he was doing something wrong and, moreover, useless. No one was in the room. It scarcely resembled the room K. had known, either. Two beds now stood one behind the other along the wall; three chairs near the door were heaped with clothes and linen; a cupboard stood open. Miss Bürstner had probably gone out while Miss Montag was talking at K. in the dining room. He was not greatly dismayed by this. He had scarcely expected any longer to meet Miss Bürstner so easily; he had made this attempt almost solely in defiance of Miss Montag. All the more embarrassing, however, was the sight, as he closed the door again, of Miss Montag and the captain talking in the open doorway of the dining room. They might have been standing there ever since K. opened the door. They avoided any appearance of watching him, spoke quietly, and followed his movements only as people glance distractedly around during a conversation. Yet those looks weighed heavily on K., and he hurried along the wall to his own room.

chapters.title: Chapter 5
paragraphs: One of the following evenings, as K. passed along the corridor between his office and the main staircase—this time he was almost the last to go home; only two attendants were still working in the dispatch office, in the small pool of light cast by an electric bulb—he heard sighs coming from behind a door where he had always supposed there was nothing but a lumber room, though he had never seen inside it. He stopped in surprise and listened again to make sure he was not mistaken. For a little while there was silence, but then the sighs came again. At first he meant to fetch one of the attendants; a witness might be useful. But then such uncontrollable curiosity seized him that he positively flung the door open. As he had rightly supposed, it was a lumber room. Useless old printed forms and empty earthenware ink bottles lying on their sides were scattered just beyond the threshold. In the room itself, however, stood three men, stooping in the low space. A candle fixed to a shelf gave them light. “What are you doing here?” K. asked, stumbling over his words in his excitement, though not loudly. One man, who evidently dominated the others and drew the eye first, was encased in a kind of dark leather garment that left his neck bare far down his chest and his arms entirely exposed. He did not answer. But the other two cried: “Sir! We're to be flogged because you complained about us to the examining magistrate.” Only now did K. recognise that they really were the guards Franz and Willem, and that the third man held a rod with which to flog them. “Well,” said K., staring at them, “I didn't complain. I only said what happened in my apartment. And your behaviour certainly wasn't beyond reproach.” “Sir,” said Willem, while Franz apparently sought protection from the third man behind him, “if you knew how badly we're paid, you'd judge us more kindly. I have a family to feed, and Franz here wanted to get married. One tries to make money however one can; work alone won't do it, even the hardest work. Your fine linen tempted me. Of course guards are forbidden to act like that; it was wrong, but it's traditional for the linen to belong to the guards. It's always been that way, believe me. And it's understandable: what do such things still mean to someone unfortunate enough to be arrested? But if he then brings it up in public, punishment has to follow.” “I didn't know what you've just told me, and I certainly didn't demand your punishment. I was concerned with a principle.” “Franz,” Willem said, turning to the other guard, “didn't I tell you the gentleman hadn't demanded our punishment? Now you hear that he didn't even know we had to be punished.” “Don't let speeches like that move you,” the third man said to K. “The punishment is as just as it is unavoidable.” “Don't listen to him,” said Willem, interrupting himself only to bring quickly to his mouth the hand that had just received a stroke of the rod. “We're only being punished because you reported us. Otherwise nothing would have happened to us, even if they'd found out what we'd done. Can that be called justice? We two, but especially I, had proved ourselves as guards over a long period—you yourself must admit that, from the authority's point of view, we guarded you well—we had prospects of advancement and would certainly soon have become floggers ourselves, like this man, who merely had the good fortune that no one reported him, because such a report is really very rare. And now, sir, everything is lost. Our careers are over; we'll have to do work far more subordinate than guarding, and on top of that we're now to receive this terribly painful flogging.” “Can the rod hurt so much?” K. asked, examining the rod the flogger swung in front of him. “We'll have to strip completely naked,” said Willem. “Oh, I see,” said K., looking closely at the flogger. He was sunburnt like a sailor and had a wild, fresh face. “Isn't there any way to spare these two the flogging?” he asked him. “No,” said the flogger, shaking his head with a smile. “Undress,” he ordered the guards. To K. he said: “You mustn't believe everything they tell you. Fear of the beating has already made them a little feeble-minded. What this one, for instance”—he pointed at Willem—“said about his possible career is downright ridiculous. Look how fat he is; the first strokes will be lost in the fat altogether. Do you know what made him so fat? He's in the habit of eating every arrested person's breakfast. Didn't he eat yours too? Well, just as I said. But a man with a belly like that can never, ever become a flogger. It's quite out of the question.” “There are floggers like that too,” Willem insisted, as he undid his trouser belt. “No,” said the flogger, drawing the rod across his neck so that he flinched. “You're supposed to be undressing, not listening.” “I'd reward you well if you let them go,” said K., taking out his wallet without looking at the flogger again; such transactions were best conducted with lowered eyes on both sides. “So you can report me too,” said the flogger, “and have me flogged as well. No, no!” “Be sensible,” said K. “If I'd wanted these two punished, I wouldn't now want to buy their freedom. I could simply slam this door, refuse to see or hear anything more and go home. But I'm not doing that. On the contrary, I'm seriously concerned to free them. If I'd suspected they were to be punished, or could even be punished, I would never have mentioned their names. I don't consider them guilty at all. The organisation is guilty; the senior officials are guilty.” “That's right!” the guards cried, and immediately received a stroke across their already bare backs. “If you had a high-ranking judge here under your rod,” said K., pressing down the rod, which was already about to rise again, as he spoke, “I certainly wouldn't stop you from striking. On the contrary, I'd give you money to strengthen you in a good cause.” “What you say sounds believable,” said the flogger, “but I don't take bribes. I'm employed to flog, so I flog.” The guard Franz, who had been fairly restrained until now, perhaps expecting K.'s intervention to succeed, now came to the door wearing only his trousers, knelt down, clung to K.'s arm and whispered: “If you can't get mercy for both of us, at least try to free me. Willem is older than I am and less sensitive in every way. He also received a light flogging once, a few years ago, but I haven't yet been disgraced, and it was only Willem who led me into behaving as I did; he's my teacher in good and bad alike. My poor fiancée is waiting down in front of the bank to see how it turns out. I'm so miserably ashamed.” He dried his tear-soaked face on K.'s jacket. “I'm not waiting any longer,” said the flogger, gripping the rod in both hands and striking Franz while Willem crouched in a corner and watched secretly, not daring to turn his head. Then Franz's scream rose, unbroken and unchanging. It seemed to come not from a human being but from a tortured instrument; the whole corridor groaned with it, the entire building must hear it. “Don't scream!” K. cried, unable to restrain himself, and while looking tensely in the direction from which the attendants would have to come, he pushed Franz, not hard but hard enough for the man, beside himself, to fall and grope convulsively over the floor with his hands. Yet he did not escape the blows; the rod found him on the ground too, and as he writhed beneath it, its tip swung regularly up and down. Already an attendant appeared in the distance, with a second a few paces behind him. K. quickly slammed the door, went to a nearby window overlooking the courtyard, and opened it. The screaming had stopped completely. To keep the attendants from approaching, he called: “It's me.” “Good evening, Mr Authorised Signatory,” came the reply. “Has something happened?” “No, no,” K. answered. “It's only a dog howling in the courtyard.” When the attendants still did not move, he added: “You can carry on with your work.” To avoid being drawn into a conversation with them, he leaned out of the window. When after a little while he looked back into the corridor, they had gone. K., however, remained at the window; he did not dare go into the lumber room, nor did he want to go home. He was looking down into a small square courtyard, surrounded by offices. All the windows were now dark; only the uppermost caught a reflection of the moon. K. strained his eyes to penetrate the darkness of a corner where several handcarts had been pushed together. It tormented him that he had not succeeded in preventing the flogging, but the failure was not his fault. If Franz had not screamed—certainly it must have hurt terribly, but at a decisive moment one has to control oneself—if he had not screamed, K. would, at least very probably, have found another way to persuade the flogger. If the entire lowest rank of officials was a rabble, why should the flogger, who held the most inhuman office, be an exception? K. had clearly observed how his eyes shone at the sight of the banknote; he had evidently made the flogging serious only to raise the bribe a little further. And K. would not have stinted. He really was concerned to free the guards; now that he had begun fighting the corruption of this judicial system, it went without saying that he would intervene on this side too. But the moment Franz began screaming, everything was naturally over. K. could not allow the attendants, and perhaps all sorts of other people, to come and surprise him negotiating with the company in the lumber room. No one could really demand such a sacrifice from K. If he had intended to make it, it would almost have been simpler to undress himself and offer himself to the flogger in the guards' place. Besides, the flogger would certainly not have accepted this substitution, since without gaining any advantage he would nevertheless have gravely violated his duty, probably doubly so, for as long as K. was subject to proceedings he must surely be inviolable to all court employees. Admittedly, special regulations might apply here too. In any case, K. had been able to do nothing but slam the door, although even now that by no means removed every danger to him. That he had finally given Franz a push as well was regrettable, excusable only by his agitation.

In the distance he heard the attendants' footsteps. To avoid attracting their attention, he closed the window and went towards the main staircase. At the lumber-room door he stopped for a little while and listened. All was quiet. The man might have flogged the guards to death; they had been entirely in his power. K. had already reached for the handle, but withdrew his hand again. He could no longer help anyone, and the attendants were bound to arrive at any moment; but he vowed to raise the matter again and, as far as lay within his power, duly punish those truly guilty, the senior officials, not one of whom had yet dared to show himself to him. As he went down the bank's outside steps, he carefully observed everyone passing, but even farther away there was no girl to be seen waiting for anyone. Franz's remark that his fiancée was waiting proved to have been a lie, though a forgivable one, whose sole purpose had been to arouse greater pity.

Even the next day K. could not get the guards out of his mind. He was distracted at work, and to finish it had to stay in the office a little longer still than the day before. When, on his way home, he again passed the lumber room, he opened it out of habit. He could not collect himself at what he saw instead of the darkness he expected. Everything was unchanged, just as he had found it when opening the door the previous evening: the printed forms and ink bottles immediately beyond the threshold, the flogger with the rod, the guards still fully dressed, the candle on the shelf. And the guards began lamenting and cried: “Sir!” K. slammed the door at once and even beat his fists against it, as though that would close it more firmly. Almost weeping, he ran to the attendants, who were working quietly at the copying machines and stopped in surprise. “Clear out the lumber room at last!” he shouted. “We're sinking in filth.” The attendants were willing to do it the following day. K. nodded; now, late in the evening, he could no longer force them to work as he had actually intended. He sat down for a little while to keep the attendants nearby, shuffled some copies out of order, believing that this gave the impression he was checking them, and then, realising that the attendants would not dare leave at the same time as he did, went home tired and without a thought.
